This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Under the premise that the ground state can be found within a specific type of function space known as the spectral Barron space, we establish that the convergence rate of the neural networks' approximation error is not reliant on the dimension $d$. Instead, we show that the error rate is determined by other parameters, such as the sample size and the complexity of the target function. Through a series of numerical experiments, we validate our theoretical findings and evaluate the generalization performance of two-layer and four-layer neural networks. Furthermore, our numerical results highlight the impact of the neural network's architecture on the estimation accuracy, training time, and computational efficiency. These experiments also compare the performance of two-layer and four-layer neural networks for two different types of perturbations. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of more complex systems and the ground state densities for one-dimensional and two-dimensional systems. Lastly, we validate the theoretical estimates of the upper and lower bounds on the generalization error. Our approaches can be adapted and generalized to other related problems. Future research directions and potential applications are also discussed. The related source code is available at https://github.com/linpengwu1217/generalization-analysis. A strong Gelfand pair (G,H) is defined by a group G and subgroup H, 
where every irreducible character of H yields a unique, multiplicity-free character of G. 
We identify all strong Gelfand pairs of the group SL(2,p) when p is a prime number, 
particularly examining the case for IR(2,p), the irreducible characters of the regular representation. 
Our results build upon prior findings by other authors who documented the Gelfand pairs of finite classical groups for smaller prime numbers. 
This information could potentially be useful for a characterisation of the group algebra of SL(2,p) when p is at most 13. 
Our approach involves determining the possible decompositions of IR(2,p) into the tensor products of irreducible characters of subgroups of SL(2,p). 
Using this knowledge, we subsequently establish the Gelfand pairs. 
Notably, these pairs include a unique Gelfand pair (SL(2,p), dihedral group D4) not previously described in the literature. 
Additionally, we document a unique Burnside triple system over fields of prime order that accommodates the minimal parabolic lift of its 2-point configuration. 
This is the first documentation of such a Burnside triple system over fields of prime order in the literature. 
Furthermore, we explore generalizations of the group algebra of SL(2,p) when p is at most 13, 
particularly exploring whether the group algebra can be expressed as a tensor product of quasiprimitive algebras. 
This exploration also applies to the group algebras of projective irreducible characters, specifically projective symplectic and projective unitary characters. 
It is found that the group algebras are the products of quasiprimitive algebras if and only if p = 2. 
Otherwise, the group algebras have an irreducible component that is isomorphic to the group algebra of a dihedral group. 
In the case of projective unitary characters, the group algebras are the products of quasiprimitive algebras if and only if p is odd. 
Otherwise, the group algebras have an irreducible component that is isomorphic to the group algebra of a quaternion group.

Specifically, we define a variant of the Gelfand--Graev module that's sensitive to regular elements in the Weyl group, apply induction to obtain a functor acting on the permutation modules parameterized by regular elements, and show that this induced functor yields the Gelfand--Graev modules for central covers. This establishes a connection between the modules and Euler--Poincar\'e polynomial of the Arnold--Bearskorn manifold. Additionally, we demonstrate how a modified version of the Weyl group's action on the induction result yields the quantum integrable module for $U_q(\mathog{sl}_2)$, thus proving a duality theory involving the Arnold--Bearskorn manifold, the Gelfand--Graev modules, and the quantum integrable module. This research generalizes prior results of E. Miller and B. K\"ulcs\'ar. Tanaka. Furthermore, we establish the classification of the irreducible modules in the category $\mathcal{MI}^{\text{ext}}(U_q(\mathog{sl}_2))$. Using advanced computer simulations, researchers studied the molecular structure of water in hexagonal ice (Ih) and low-density amorphous ice (LDA) at low temperatures under high pressure. When subjected to this pressure, both types of ice transform into a high-density amorphous ice (HDA) in a sudden, drastic phase transition. An innovative measure, based on the arrangement of oxygen atoms in the system, allowed the researchers to detect the presence of small, intact IH-Ih crystal clusters embedded within the resulting HDA ice, which formed immediately before it transformed into LDA. These fragile, multi-ring crystal structures, comprising 16-32 oxygen atoms, disappeared quickly, within a few picoseconds, and left behind a large, structurally unstable and disordered LDA ice. Interestingly, a comparable phenomenon was also detected when starting with a tetrahedral high-density amorphous ice (HD-A) and allowing it to transform into a low-density amorphous ice (LD-A). However, the resulting LDA ice lacked any detectable crystal clusters during its formation. An associated phase diagram illustrates how varying degrees of thermal stability are linked to distinct arrangements of molecular bonds in different types of ice. Notably, high-density amorphous ice exhibits unique, fragile crystal domains, whereas low-density amorphous ice does not, explaining why it is relatively more stable and resists transformation at low temperatures. The investigation into the Local Density of States (LDS) of materials employs Scanning Tunnelling Microscopy (STM) to create highly-resolved images of atomic structures. This research utilized an STM to study three materials: graphite, gold and silicon. The aim of this experiment was to acquire atomic-resolution images of the atomic structures in order to calculate their respective LDS curves. A multi-step calibration process was employed to achieve reliable results, encompassing the determination of tunneling conditions, atom identification, and ultimately, experimental determination of the LDS curves. A variety of images were taken for each material, with a focus on selecting a single, high-quality atom for the STM measurements. A unique and unexplained phenomenon was observed during the imaging of graphite, characterized by a random and rapid change in tunneling resistance. An explanation for this behavior, attributed to a tunneling mechanism involving a three-electron process, is presented. A comparative analysis of the experimentally-derived LDS curves with established results demonstrated that our findings were consistent with existing literature, culminating in the generation of data suitable for use in Quantum Point Contact devices. This involves four techniques for converting magnetic field data into audio, whose applications will be examined along with discussions of relevant tools and how to listen to ultralow frequency waves. By reinterpreting data through audio visualization, researchers can uncover new patterns and contextually dependent meanings that might otherwise go undetected in traditional plots. This listening tour will serve as a springboard for future research into the development of more sophisticated methods for converting magnetospheric data into audio, potentially including machine learning algorithms for categorizing wave types or identifying plasma instabilities based on their oscillatory patterns. Research using audio visualization has shown that ULF wave patterns hold clues about the equilibrium of the plasma, while specific types of waves may be associated with particular instabilities or processes. This research aims to further refine and expand the use of audio visualization as a diagnostic tool for uncovering new insights into magnetospheric wave activity. Ultimately, by reimagining the way we interact with time-series data, we may uncover critical information about the plasma and its various processes. This research marks a step towards making the heliosphere an audible place. Listening to the plasma can uncover new insights into the equilibrium, while converting magnetic field data into audio may reveal more detailed information about the physical mechanisms at work. This approach to understanding data holds potential for further development, whether it's exploring the Sun's atmosphere or the world of quantum mechanics. Despite the significant advancements, these systems still struggle with text comprehension, essentially treating text as data rather than knowledge. We introduce a novel text representation framework grounded in declarative memory, leveraging concepts inspired by human long-term memory to improve language processing algorithms and enhance their performance. We validate the effectiveness of this framework through experimental comparisons with existing methods on three datasets. The phenomenon of the Pauli Exclusion Principle manifests itself when low-temperature 2D harmonic oscillator traps hold fermions at the ground state. As a result, the lack of interaction between fermions leads to the formation of Pauli crystals. This research aims to understand this occurrence by using statistical mechanics to determine the energy and dimensions of a non-interacting arrangement of ultra-cold fermions, combining two theories - fermion degeneracy and harmonic oscillator treatment. This unification of perspectives provides a more complete and reliable explanation for the characteristics of Pauli crystals. Additionally, the models used in this analysis are versatile and can be applied to a variety of fermion ensembles, including those created from alkali metals and rare earth atoms. Statistical mechanics offers a beneficial framework for interpreting the physical interactions involved in the formation of Pauli crystals. This approach is beneficial for the development of experiments and the evaluation of their results. Furthermore, the dimensions of Pauli crystals can be used to calculate the strength of the external confinement and identify any unaccounted for interactions between fermions. This analysis is particularly useful for understanding the development of Pauli crystals from newly discovered 2D fermion systems. Studies of these novel systems, such as those formed from Yb and Ce atoms, have the potential to significantly advance our understanding of the interactions involved. This research provides a clear distinction between the physical interactions and the geometric characteristics of Pauli crystals, similar to existing theories. However, this distinction is complicated in the evaluation of experimental results, leading to incorrect assumptions about the strength of interactions between fermions, specifically regarding phase transitions within Pauli crystals. One such incorrect assumption was made by N. Manfredi et al. regarding the strength of interactions between Ce atoms, who incorrectly linked their results to the geometric characteristics of Pauli crystals through an incorrect analogy. On the other hand, the analysis of Cs atoms, who have well understood interactions, provides a reliable explanation for the dimensions of their Pauli crystals. This is in contrast to newly discovered 2D fermion systems, who have poorly understood interactions and require a more in-depth analysis. The unique nature of Pauli crystals to geometric and physical perspectives highlights their potential as a valuable system for the investigation of the intricate relationships between these principles. Ultimately, the unique characteristics and applications of Pauli crystals provide a compelling argument for the continued exploration and understanding of these fascinating many-body systems. Transmission system operators utilize unit commitment as crucial tools for determining the most cost-effective and feasible generation schedules. Researchers have been investigating constraint screening, a technique that can expedite the solution process for large-scale unit commitment problems by reducing the number of unnecessary constraints. Current constraint screening methods, however, necessitate a quadratic optimization model and often involve computationally demanding processes. In response, this study presents a novel approach for constraint screening and loading using an machine learning-based cost model instead of quadratic optimization. The proposed cost model can be rapidly trained from historical data and employed to efficiently screen constraints. Experimental evaluations on large-scale datasets have demonstrated the efficacy of this method in reducing constraint counts by up to 40% and lowering solution times of commercial optimization software by up to 35% without compromising feasibility. Notably, this technique can successfully apply constraint loading, disabling unnecessary constraints and significantly reducing computational costs. The study also compares constraint screening and loading on real-world datasets, highlighting that constraint screening is more effective for problems with fewer feasible solutions, whereas loading is better suited for larger feasible sets. The proposed method has been successfully tested on datasets with over 2000 hours and 500 units without any reduction in feasibility, and is expected to perform even more optimally on even larger datasets. The accompanying code is available on GitHub under the repository https://github.com/uis-rcs/learn_cm_uc. The learned cost models can also be accessed via https://uis-rcs.github.io/learn_cm_uc. The proposed method is expected to have a range of potential applications, limiting its use to these areas: constraint screening and loading for unit commitment, power system operations and planning. The accompanying models and datasets are as specified above, under the tabs 'learn_cm_uc' and 'datasets'. The proposed cost model is available as the Python package 'learn_cm_uc' in the above repository. The accompanying data samples are available in the above repository. The proposed method does not employ deep learning, using an alternative approach as described in the abstract. The corresponding author of the paper is Tyler Halder. Our research presents a multi-dimensional particle-in-cell study on how an extremely powerful laser interacts with a plasma containing charged particles. We specifically examined what happens when a very short, powerful laser pulse travels through a plasma with a high density, resulting in a high electric field beyond the relativistic threshold. Our simulations show that the laser pulse undergoes shock-like behavior as it plows through the plasma, inducing current and charge density fluctuations that generate an intense transverse electric field. This intense field can reverse the direction of the electric field inside the laser, causing electron injection into the head of the laser pulse. By manipulating the degree of laser frequency chirp, we were able to control both the electron injection rate and the peak energy reached by electrons during the acceleration process. Furthermore, simultaneous changes in the electron injection location and time allowed us to achieve simultaneous acceleration and deceleration populations of electrons, resulting in a range of final energies extending from thousands to hundreds of thousands of electronvolts. To investigate these properties, we employed the characteristics of the system when reduced under spatial symmetry and demonstrated the conservation of the $N$-th power of the smooth horizon volume, an insight derived from the Maxwell equation. Two related variations of the well-known knapsack problem are the Set-Union Knapsack Problem and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem. Both involve selecting items from a set to maximize an objective while adhering to a budget limit and a set of nonnegative item values, as well as elements weighted for coverage. We propose a novel algorithm, E2LS, specifically designed to solve these two problems efficiently, making it a pioneering solution that simultaneously addresses both. By introducing a novel search operator called ADD$^*$, E2LS strikes a balance between exploration and efficiency in the search region. Furthermore, E2LS employs the tabu search strategy to avoid local maxima, thus ensuring its thorough exploration of the solution space. Comprehensive tests across 168 publicly available problem instances showcase the remarkable performance of the proposed algorithm in solving both the SUKP and BMCP. The results indicate that E2LS achieves an average improvement of 22.1% in solution value when compared to the currently best available solution, thus solidifying its effectiveness. Additionally, E2LS consistently outperforms its counterparts by solving over 90% of the tested instances in less than 160 seconds. As a result of its superior performance, E2LS remarkably reduces the gap between the known upper and lower bounds for both the SUKP and BMCP in more than 95% of the tested cases, thus leading to a notable bound improvement of at most 4.4%. The empirical outcomes of our research highlight the practical utility of E2LS as a robust and efficient computational solution for both the SUKP and BMCP. Moreover, we utilize E2LS to demonstrate that both the SUKP and BMCP can be efficiently transformed into one another in a straightforward manner. Finally, based on our extensive computational results, we derive new lower bounds for both problems, thus contributing to the theoretical advancement of these challenging computational problems. The proposed algorithm, along with additional computational data and source code, are freely accessible via our provided website. The experimental evaluation of our approach not only strengthens the theoretical findings for both the SUKP and BMCP but also significantly enhances their practical applicability and applicators' confidence. Ultimately, we thoroughly test and verify the theoretical properties for both problems, thus contributing meaningfully to their literature. Recent studies have suggested using total correlation to measure functional connectivity between brain regions as a more comprehensive alternative to conventional pair-wise measures such as correlation and mutual information. Building on this concept, we developed a whole brain connectivity network based on total correlation and demonstrated its potential to serve as an imaging biomarker for brain alterations. Specifically, we employed data from the Human Connectome Project and found that regional levels of total correlation exhibit significant and consistent patterns of correlation with demographic traits, even after adjusting for correlations of the same trait across different regions, a phenomenon known as "pre-whitening". This finding highlights the inherent structure in total correlation networks, revealing their collective behavior and hinting at a relationship between this correlation measure and brain function. Moreover, we identified significant correlations between total correlation based functional connectivity and demographic traits, even after accounting for individual-wise "pre-whitening" and adjusting for correlations of the same trait across different regions. Notably, we found substantial correlations between total correlation and age, as well as modest correlations with sex and Onset Age, while no significant correlations were detected for other demographic traits. Importantly, the established relationships between total correlation and demographic traits hold true at varying scales, further emphasizing the inherent structure in total correlation networks. Moreover, we found significant community structure in the total correlation matrix at a coarse scale, which was able to capture the relationships between total correlation and demographic traits with high accuracy. This suggests that total correlation provides valuable insights into brain organization and function. Finally, we proposed methods to construct consistent and reproducible functional connectivity networks from independent subjects, even in small dataset sizes, by employing a coarse-grained approach that retains the established structural relationships. This approach is expected to enhance our understanding of the whole brain connectivity and its implications for brain function and diseases. Moreover, the developed methods can be easily adapted for other multivariate measures and datasets, enabling us to construct reliable functional connectivity networks even in small to medium-sized datasets. Ultimately, the established relationships between total correlation and demographic traits are robust and consistent, making total correlation based functional connectivity a valuable tool for whole brain analysis and providing new insights into brain organization and function. Furthermore, the established methods can be widely applied for whole brain analysis beyond total correlation, while the established relationships between total correlation and demographic traits are specific to the employed measure and dataset, providing novel and significant insights into brain organization and function. The classical Segal-Bargmann theory explores three key Hilbert space unitary 
isomorphisms that explain the dual nature of waves and particles and the 
interplay between configuration space and phase space. This work extends the 
Segal-Bargmann theory to a Clifford Algebra context, focusing on a specific 
version of the theory that uses Taylor series expansions within the Clifford 
Algebra. The resulting unitary isomorphisms involve various geometric structures 
on manifolds, incorporating both Euclidean and Minkowski cases. In addition, 
the proof of this extended theory is tied to the isomorphism between Taylor 
expansion and the Meixner formula, resulting in a concise and unified proof of 
the isomorphisms. This work also provides an appendix examining Clifford Algebra 
probability measures and their connection to fermionic Gaussian states. An 
important property of these measures is their invariance under Clifford Algebra 
clifford reflections, which serve as a Clifford Algebra analogue to the phase 
rotation invariance of Bose Gaussian states within the Segal-Bargmann framework. 
As a consequence, the volume elements in this context turn out to be invariant 
under such Clifford reflections. They serve as a key element in the extended 
Segal-Bargmann theory and are central to the geometric structures involved. The 
appendix explores their properties and connections to fermionic Gaussian states, 
and discusses a potential loss of positivity issue for these measures, which 
arises when certain conditions on their parameters are not met, resulting in 
non-probability distributions being used in this framework. A simple polynomial 
invariant expression is proposed to avoid this issue, tying the Segal-Bargmann 
theory to a Ginzburg-Landau model with a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry breaking term. 
Ultimately, the main contribution of this work is the derivation and exploration 
of the geometric structures involved in the unitary isomorphisms, which serve 
as a unified and concise theory, and serve as a standalone contribution even 
in the classical real case. The accompanying supplementary materials include 
Julia code for the main computations in this work.

Research on top tagging has advanced rapidly due to the top quark's substantial role in studying physics that goes beyond the standard model. Recent studies have concentrated on boosting top tagging techniques to increase their sensitivity to new physics. We employed two modern machine learning methods, mean shift clustering and neural density estimation, to develop boosted top tagging classifiers. By incorporating these tools into a multistage classification process, we significantly enhanced the top tagging tags' accuracy compared to current methods. We also utilized the Shapley value to illustrate how individual discriminative tags contribute to the classification results. By examining the Shapley values, we can determine the most valuable information in the input data that contributes to the classification result, and our work confirms that the Shapley value can identify tags previously believed to be uninformative that are still valuable in the final classification. Furthermore, the Shapley value analysis reveals the time-dependent tags' contribution to the classification result, and our work shows that the multistage topology of the tags and their interdependence can increase the overall classification result. We also demonstrate that the neural density estimation classifier is more sensitive to collider constraints than the mean shift clustering classifier. Finally, we demonstrate that the boosted top tagging tools can be used to analyze current and future collider data and produce a significant increase in sensitivity to top quark pair resonances. The boosted top tagging tools and our multistage multivariate analysis can be applied to various future collider experiments and data collection strategies to increase their sensitivity to new physics. We also show that the combination of the top tagging tags' time-dependent properties provides the most significant constraints on time-dependent resonance cross sections and production rates. Theoretical particles called heavy neutral leptons have the potential to resolve long-standing problems in physics, particularly those related to neutrino oscillations. These particles, being unable to interact with the standard model in the same way as other particles, could have Majorana masses that allow for a violation of lefthanded symmetry. Experiments can indirectly search for this property by looking for evidence of processes called neutrinoless double-beta decays. Our study addresses the efficient verification problem, specifically the $k = 1, 2,$ and $3$ round cases, for a universal quantum algorithm, called Abelian hidden shift, by developing an algorithm that generates a certificate and sends it once, or in three rounds with an intermediate re-certification, allowing for highly likely successful verification with $n$ or $n/2 + O(\log n)$ rounds and degrees of freedom in the first and second cases respectively. By employing this advanced representation, which utilizes a transformer-based model, a significant improvement in localization performance has been achieved for complex 3D environments. The resulting approach, known as NDT-Transformer, surpasses state-of-the-art methods by achieving a 5.0% point cloud localization accuracy on the SUN3D dataset, a large-scale benchmark for 3D point cloud localization. Furthermore, this technique enables real-time localization, even when working with large-scale datasets, making it well-suited for applications in autonomous vehicles, robotics, and geographic information systems. By integrating depth information, an additional increase in precision can be obtained. The resulting NDT-Transformer method enables the development of highly accurate and efficient 3D point cloud localization models, which have the potential to transform various applications in robotics, geographic information systems, and computer-aided engineering. The accompanying code has been implemented using the Pytorch and Open3d libraries, making it accessible to the research community. A series of qualitative experiments have been performed to validate the proposed approach, which demonstrates its ability to accurately localize 3D point clouds in a wide range of complex and realistic environments. The resulting models, which can be trained in a semi-supervised or self-supervised manner, have the potential to significantly contribute to the research community. mainly driven by the widespread use of language blending in social media across 
multi-lingual countries such as India, Mexico, Europe, and parts of Africa. 
Language models have shown particular difficulty with positional encoding in 
code-mixed text processing, leading to the adoption of static positional 
encodings regardless of word position. To address this limitation, we introduce 
PESTO, a novel approach that dynamically encodes positionally significant words 
using a switching mechanism that adapts based on word type (lemma, prefix, 
suffix, etc.). We represent word position in a novel relative encoding format 
and evaluate our approach through experiments on publicly available datasets 
for categorization tasks in language pairs including Hindi-English, Sanskrit- 
English, and Romanized Hindi-English, achieving notable improvements in accuracy 
over static positional encoding in all cases. The data and models can be accessed 
through the link https://github.com/earskystream/pesto_code_mixed_encodings.

  1. Introducing a dynamic positional encoding approach, PESTO, for enhanced 
  encoding effectiveness.
  2. Proposing a relative positional encoding format for increased 
  interpretability and lemmatization efficiency.
  3. Overcoming the limitations of static positional encoding in current 
  language models with promising results on code-mixed datasets.

on positional encodings in language modeling for code-mixed texts and

This paper presents an innovative technique to create spatial boundaries for navigation around moving obstacles in dynamic environments. In the field of autonomous driving and robotics, motion planning is a fundamental challenge. Many current methods leverage geometric constraints to limit search spaces for potential paths. However, traditional geometric constraints often fall short in handling complex environments characterized by large speeds, high densities, and diverse shapes of moving obstacles. To address this limitation, we developed a novel constraint synthesis approach that leverages flow-based geometry to isolate valid areas for navigation. Our proposed method has been successfully tested and validated against state-of-the-art motion planning tools in various dynamic scenarios. Results show that the new constraint generation approach yields substantially shorter average path lengths of up to 15% compared to the global planner BT, notable improvements in constraint tightness of up to 10%, and comparable or even improved computational efficiency. Our technique has been successfully integrated into the Autowaymate autonomous driving system. Following a one-year integration period, the new constraint generation approach led to notable performance improvements during real-world driving tests. Specifically, the average search volume decreased by 28%, the average computation time declined by 13%, and the success rates of the global planner increased by 3-5%. Our technique is now being used in production as the standard motion planning constraint in the Autowaymate system. We plan to further develop and extend this work in future directions. For instance, the new constraint generation approach could be applied to other robotics and autonomous driving systems to enhance overall performance. Additionally, the underlying mathematical concepts from flow-based geometry can be leveraged to develop novel constraint synthesis methods for a range of open-world challenges. Our work may also contribute to the creation of more sophisticated robot motion planning algorithms, as well as the advancement of autonomous driving systems through the integration of flow-based geometry techniques. Our technique is poised to continue making a significant impact in the fields of robotics and autonomous driving systems. This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel maps. A hierarchical descriptor, developed using deep neural networks, is employed to analyze image features at various scales. Localizing the camera involves two key steps: either matching a single key image or reconstructing a short sequence of key images based on key points identified in the current image. To refine the estimated pose, pointcloud pruning is performed in conjunction with deep network-based 2D-3D matching. The proposed approach is evaluated using the KITTI benchmark, yielding state-of-the-art results for 2D-2D matching. Furthermore, it demonstrates superior performance compared to other methods when incorporating 2D-3D matching for both 2D-2D and 2D-3D matching scenarios. To the best of our knowledge, this technique represents the first visual relocalization approach leveraging 3D surfel maps and hierarchical descriptors. As a result, it significantly outperforms methods solely relying on point clouds, achieving scene-agnostic performance comparable to unsupervised learning-based methods. We establish a condition ensuring that any reversible Markov process necessarily converges to its associated reversible stationary process. We demonstrate, however, that this convergence may occur at different rates for various reversible stationary distributions. Furthermore, through an example involving random walks across distinct graphs, we illustrate the possibility of significant variation in convergence rates. Uniformly, the large-sample convergence of any Markov process to its stationary distribution has been established by various authors [18, 8, 17, 14]; however, our research focuses specifically on the convergence of these processes to their stationary distributions. Our primary result is a strong, general condition for this convergence, which is discussed in Section 1. Examples of processes meeting this condition are illustrated in Section 2. The initial half of this section involve general findings regarding reversible Markov processes, while the latter concern random walks across dynamic graphs. The main proof of our condition is presented in Section 3. The conclusion of our research involves discussion of our results in relation to existing literature. The proof of a key lemma requiring a Fourier analysis is included as an appendix. One of the widely applied machine learning algorithms is logistic regression, often used for binary classification tasks. Despite its straightforward nature, logistic regression can be computationally intensive, particularly when applied to large datasets. To streamline communication and avoid it when possible, we've developed a method called Asynchronous Stochastic Gradient Descent with optimized memory management (ASGD-M). This approach keeps memory usage low while allowing ASGD to learn and update parameters independently, avoiding the need for communication. Our results show that ASGD-M, when compared to standard asynchronous stochastic gradient descent, still achieves comparable convergence, but with reduced communication and memory usage. To further improve performance, we've discovered that logistic regression can be run on devices with limited memory by breaking down class parameters into individual components and distributing them evenly, effectively doubling the available memory and reducing communication needs. This approach, known as Expanded Memory Optimization (EMO), enables efficient execution on devices with limited memory under communication constraints. Our experiments confirm that EMO leads to significant improvements in convergence, outperforming existing methods like weight decoupling and Mirrored Modes. To facilitate seamless deployment on distributed systems, we've also developed a customizable execution policy called Stratified Execution (SE). This policy ensures that execution is stratified based on the presence of gradients and updates, enabling a flexible and efficient execution model that balances device availability and usage to optimize the whole system. Our results show that when combined with EMO, SE leads to a substantial 5.6 times improvement in convergence over the baseline method. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents a novel approach for optimizing communication and memory in machine learning algorithms, specifically logistic regression. Our method's generalizability has been confirmed through testing it on various large-scale open-source datasets, and our results suggest that it can be effectively applied to a broader range of machine learning tasks. However, the method's applicability to tasks involving deep learning models remains an area for further research. Our findings indicate that such models may require modifications in their parameter structure to achieve efficient execution on devices with limited memory. The research's data sources include a variety of large-scale open-source datasets, and the research's performance has been benchmarked against the state-of-the-art Solving BNS Solvers algorithm. The research's scope was specifically on communication optimization, and a more comprehensive study of machine learning algorithms' memory usage remains an area for further research

Future large-scale radio interferometers, such as the Square Kilometer Array, will likely have numerous antennas with hundreds of antennas per side, leading to significant computational complexity when processing individual data streams. To mitigate this, we explore new calibration algorithms that take advantage of the regular grid structure, allowing for efficient division of calculations into smaller, independent components. By breaking down the 2D Fourier transform into 1D components and leveraging previously established baseline Fourier transforms, we can significantly reduce the computational complexity from the traditional O(N^2) scale to O(N log N). This breakthrough allows large-scale interferometers to maintain rapid data processing speeds despite the vast number of antennas. Furthermore, our novel calibration algorithms ensure accurate and reliable calibration across the regular grid, even with numerous antennas. While implementing these algorithms requires more intricate code, the underlying computational concept is straightforward and can be applied to designs of next-generation radio interferometers.  Specifically we demonstrate several protocols that achieve a computational complexity of $N\log{N}$.  One of the protocols uses $N$ FFTs sized $\sqrt{N}$ and $2\log{N}$ FFTs sized $\log^{2}{N}$.  An alternative uses $\log^{2}{N}$ FFTs sized $\log^{2}{N}$.  We note that although these algorithms achieve a higher computational complexity than traditional methods, the margin of difference increases with the size of the interferometer.  To bring this concept to practical use, we have developed a prototype implementation in C++ that takes advantage of the CUDA framework.  This prototype demonstrates the feasibility of this concept by reducing the computational complexity from O(N^2) to O(N log N) while maintaining high performance.  Specifically for an FFT size of 8192 we see a 5:1 ratio of computational complexity, for 81920 we see a 20:1, and for 819200 we see approximately 80:1.  These results indicate the potential for large-scale interferometers to maintain rapid data processing speeds despite the vast number of antennas.  An implementation in hardware would be expected to yield an even greater margin of difference.  This work represents an important step towards making large-scale radio interferometers a practical reality.  An implementation in hardware and a software proof-of-concept have been initiated to bring the concept to completion.  A patent has been filed. A widely accepted method for measuring investment portfolio diversification is the mean variance strategy. However, this approach has limitations, particularly regarding its assumption that asset returns adhere to specific, non-essential distribution assumptions. In reality, these assumptions often don't hold. As a result, more advanced machine learning based methods have been suggested in recent times. These methods, however, face several challenges including difficulty in training, limited interpretation of results, and highly complex nature. In this paper, an alternative approach to the previous ones is proposed. This proposal involves a new metric for evaluating portfolio diversification called Information Achievable Portfolio Allocation, and a novel Autoencoding Conditional Generative model based approach. The proposed approach follows a two-step process. First, it identifies optimal portfolio allocations based on a desired level of risk using the proposed information metric. Next, an Autoencoding Conditional Generative model is trained to generate portfolios with reduced dimensionality, and a new metric to measure overfitting. Experiments were conducted using simulated data as well as real data from the S&P 500 index, and the results show promising outcomes. These results include reduced loss in most cases for both training and test data indicating minimal overfitting, and average loss scores ranging from 2 to 4 for the test data. These scores show that the proposed model is capable of effectively capturing interasset correlations and generating more informative portfolio allocations. Moreover, the proposed approach offers several benefits including enhanced generalization to unknown environments, reduced overfitting, and improved transparency and colloborative setup. All these benefits were lacking in previous works or the proposed system with these defects being too complex. Therefore, the proposed work breaks this limitation. Finally, future research directions are suggested in the paper. One key area for further exploration is the extension of this approach to other financial problems. This could potentially lead to new and complex value creation opportunities. The corresponding code can be found at https://github.com/andreab/ACAlico. We have derived the polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$
analytically to three-loop order in QCD for arbitrary values of $N$.
The result holds for any value of $N$, including those not previously considered.
This provides the basis for the calculation of the polarized structure function $g_1^{a}(x)$
in the variable flavor number scheme at four-loop order.
We have also obtained the large $N$ limit of the matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$
and compared it to the corresponding two-loop results for the massive operator $O_{gq}^{(2)}(M)$
as well as to the results of differential equations.
Furthermore, the two-loop massive and two-loop small-$N$ finite matrix elements were previously determined. 
This comparison allows us to verify previously derived two-loop results for the massive operator $O_{gq}^{(2)}(M)$
and to obtain the results for the polarized massive operator $O_{\psi1_{+}}^{(2)}(M)$
which was not previously known.
Using the correct two-loop expression for $A_{qq}^{(2)}(M)$
we correct an error made in a related paper. 
The correct two-loop expressions for all the scale-dependent part of the polarized structure functions allow
the construction of the four-loop asymptotic perturbative expansion for the structure function $g_1^{a}(x)$
which is the most accurate to date. 
This is achieved by combining the correct two-loop expressions with three-loop corrections
and the knowledge of the leading and next-to-leading terms in $1/N$.
The resulting four-loop corrections are known to be the most complete and accurate to date. 
This is accompanied by the knowledge of the correct two-loop corrections and the leading terms in $1/N$.
Additionally, the present paper provides the leading contribution to the construction of the four-loop corrections
due to the knowledge of the correct two-loop expressions for the massive operator $O_{\psi1_{+}}(M)$
and the $\gamma2$-function. 
This is crucial since these two-loop expressions are not previously known. 
Finally, the present paper provides the first numerical results for the structure function $g_1^{a(3)}(x)$
and the leading term in $1/N$, allowing for the comparison with experimental data

Several of the most widely applied equations for relating temperature, specific humidity, and virtual specific humidity in moist air calculations come with significant issues.
The primary problem is an inconsistent thermodynamic representation, specifically with regards to the relationship between specific heat capacity and temperature.
We have examined multiple sets of equations that attempt to account for the effects of water vapour and liquid in air, including those that apply approximations to virtual specific humidity.
We identified four distinct sets of equations that represent a consistent thermodynamic approach.
These sets of equations were then used to investigate changes in enthalpy and internal energy in various test scenarios.
The results showed that only one version of the equations, specifically with the effects of water vapour and liquid included in the enthalpy, yielded results that matched exactly across all test scenarios.
Furthermore, the analysis revealed that the interaction between water vapour, liquid, and solid phases within the thermodynamic model is negligible, and can thus be disregarded.
We also derived specific versions of the equations that take into consideration the effects of water vapour and liquid, and provided conversion formulas to adapt existing models to the new thermodynamic representation.
The application of the derived versions of the equations to atmospheric modelling is discussed in this study. Further research is required to investigate their practical implications in various fields, including modelling of the atmosphere and cryosphere. We introduce algebraic objects, which generalise ordered semirings and monoids, and extend these to objects that include elements acting as negative identities. An exterior algebra analogue is proposed, which provides a cryptomorphism for matroids, and shows that standard exterior and idempotent exterior algebras can be derived from it under specific conditions. A broad class of algebraic objects is identified, which satisfies all necessary conditions to serve as a generalised base for matroid representation. An algebraic object that is the exterior analogue of a partial semiring is also proposed, which provides a cryptomorphism for transversal matroids. Furthermore, it's demonstrated that several well-known cryptomorphisms can be derived from the proposed algebraic objects, and through example, it's illustrated that these proposed objects can encompass multiple previously defined objects within a unified framework. An efficient and direct algorithmic approach is proposed for solving combinatorial problems, which generalises the Gaussian elimination algorithm, and also reveals that solving problems in one domain can provide insights for solving similar problems in another domain, thus potentially solving problems more efficiently. Lastly, additional properties and results of the proposed algebraic objects and their mappings are obtained. In addition to matroids and transversal matroids, first results are also provided for more complex objects such as laminar matroids and cographic matroids, and this potential for further generalisation to larger objects is acknowledged. In addition to the theoretical contributions, experimental results are provided that test the efficiency of the proposed solutions, and suggestions are made for future work that integrates these proposed solutions to complement existing methods. Research on interpreting the outcomes of automatic speech recognition for conversational tracking has been largely neglected. This study examines the impact of ASR misinterpretation on the performance of a conversational tracking model and proposes an approach to assess the likelihood of different ASR translations from a single audio input. By applying a confusion network model to this process, the model's ambiguity can be measured and the model's performance optimized in the presence of this confusion. Experimental results show that by taking the confusion network into consideration, the model's performance is improved, with gains of up to 6.8% observed in the strict metric, at no extra cost in the loose metric. Furthermore, when the confusion network is used to select the most optimal hypothesis among a range of possible translations, the model's performance is significantly improved, with gains of up to 13.2% observed in the strict metric. This represents an 8.3% increase in the combination of both strict and loose metrics. The complete model is available for use through the CNUDST tool in the Sparsity Pyramid Library. 2020 IEEE. This invariance aligns with vector bundles when certain conditions, including r and d being coprime, are met. A critical factor in secret sharing schemes is the count of minimal qualified subsets, as knowing this value results in the richest possible access structure. Specifically, this structure contains participants in all feasible Boolean combinations of the minimal qualified subsets, yielding the maximum complexity given the number of subsets. Every access structure can be considered a subset of this universal structure when having the same number of minimal qualified subsets, thereby the universal access structure with $n$ minimal qualified subsets, denoted by $\mathcal{A}_{n}$, holds the record for the highest complexity for any access structure. Previous work by Shamir and van Dam established a lower bound on the complexity of $\mathcal{A}_{n}$ of $\Omega(n^2/\binom{k}{(n-1)/2})$ for an access structure with $n$ minimal qualified subsets and a central point $k$ when the size of the universal structure is significantly larger than the lower bound. However, for smaller $n$ and $k$ values with a central point, the problem of the complexity of $\mathcal{A}_{n}$ remained unsolved. This work presents an improved complexity bound of $n^2/(n+1)^2$ for the universal access structure with $n$ minimal qualified subsets and a central point $k = (n+1)/2$, thereby resolving the problem and advancing the previously established complexity bound of $\mathcal{A}_{n}$ to a higher magnitude with a more pronounced magnitude for any access structure with $n$ minimal qualified subsets and a central point close to $n/2$. Additionally, this work describes how to achieve the high complexity of $\mathcal{A}_{15}$ with 15 minimal qualified subsets, using the recently developed $(q, n-q)$-secret-sharing scheme of Wang et al. (2020) for any access structure with 15 minimal qualified subsets. However, for larger $n$ values, the problem of the complexity of $\mathcal{A}_{n}$ for an access structure with 15 minimal qualified subsets and a central point remained unsolved. This work presents an advanced secret-sharing scheme allowing the creation of $\mathcal{A}_{15}$ with 15 minimal qualified subsets and a complexity of 256, thereby overcoming an issue in Wang et al.'s scheme and advancing the previously established complexity bound of $\mathcal{A}_{n}$ to a higher magnitude with a more pronounced magnitude for any access structure with 15 minimal qualified subsets. To determine entanglement experimentally in polarization qubit pairs, we utilize quantum estimation theory to develop the most precise estimators possible, which we then apply to achieve maximum fidelity when simulating Bell measurements. We show that these optimal estimators are variance minimizers and derive mathematical formulas for their precision. Crucially, we find that achieving these optimal values does not necessitate fine tuning to an exact target value, but rather allows for practical implementation within a predictable error range. These estimators are further adapted for tomography, enabling accurate Bell measurement matrices to be accurately estimated within certain margins. We successfully implement these concepts in experimental settings, using either simulated or real Bell measurements. We demonstrate that our approach can accurately simulate Bell measurements with high precision, even when realizations are limited to hundreds of repeats. Furthermore, we apply this method to accurately estimate the coefficients of Bell states in a four-state vector, \eta_{\mathbf{B}}. The results validate the effectiveness of this method in entanglement simulation and suggest its applicability to more complex scenarios. We anticipate that this technique will be applied to entanglement distribution and quantum computing protocols involving multiple particles. We also provide a perspective on potential applications to entanglement measurement and quantum information processing. The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic after their initial discovery in 2017. A thorough investigation into their characteristics has been completed using detailed edge plasma measurements and advanced computer simulations. PTMs were identified using edge plasma frequency measurements and characterized, showing they are stationary in the turbulence frame. Data collected during various experiments and edge plasma conditions indicate that these stationary patterns persist across different edge plasma densities. To further understand the origin of PTM, researchers analyzed multiple aspects but were unable to make any conclusive findings regarding their cause. However, our study reveals that PTM exhibit properties consistent with edgetic bursts, which often border the inner edge of the edge plasma. A detailed computer simulation, which mimics the edge plasma behavior of JET, was used to test various scenarios and demonstrated that PTM can arise from long-lasting edgetic bursts. Although this model does not provide a definitive explanation for all observed data, it successfully accounts for the majority of the observed features of PTMs in JET's edge plasma. A more in-depth exploration of this origin is recommended to confirm this preliminary finding. Additionally, our study highlights the significance of using advanced techniques, such as Edgetronics, to better understand plasma behavior at the edge of magnetic confinement devices like JET. By combining detailed measurements of the edge plasma with computer simulations, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of complex phenomena like those observed in JET's edge plasma. Importantly, these methods and models can be applied to other areas of plasma research. Although this study primarily focuses on palm tree modes in the JET tokamak, it is generally applicable to other areas of plasma research, which is one of the key takeaways from this work. Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of leveraging pre-trained models by comparing a straightforward, high-filter-size convolution baseline with more complex models that build upon the pre-trained models. We apply these approaches to two continual learning tasks - continual learning with a focus on feature learning, and semi-superpixel-based continual learning. Our results show that a convolutional model with a large number of filters (e.g. CConv5) can match or outperform more complex models, including models based on pre-trained models such as ResNet, in both tasks. When the models are allowed to learn from the data, a convolutional model with a large number of filters shows better performance and stability in both tasks, including a reduction in performance loss and an increased rate of performance growth. Additionally, we show that a convolutional model with a large number of filters can be used to improve the performance of other approaches that build upon the pre-trained models, leading to increased performance and stability. Overall, our results highlight the significance of utilizing pre-trained models as well as a robust, high-filter-size convolutional model as a simple yet effective baseline for continual learning. As social media increasingly influences public discourse, developers are working to infrequently update sophisticated AI models that can recognize hate speech on various platforms. Although models like these are being used, researchers have neglected to investigate the specific features and components of these models, making them harder to improve. Our research addresses this by proposing a unified framework that can process text and other forms of media to identify hate speech. We examined the importance of individual model components, such as visual and text-based components, features, and architectures, through a series of experiments involving a hate speech classification dataset and an associated leaderboard. By conducting an in-depth analysis and leveraging explanation techniques, we were able to identify key image characteristics that contribute to our model's accuracy. Our results show that our approach, which uses a pre-trained vision model and a more flexible text encoding method, is more effective than current state-of-the-art methods. When we remove specific image regions, our model's accuracy decreases, with the most significant decline occurring in image subsections where hate-related content is present. These findings suggest that our model is better equipped to identify hate speech in images than text-based models. We have made our code available on GitHub, including the updated model and guidelines for interpreting image results. We plan to expand on this research by exploring more techniques for understanding and improving the accuracy of these models. One such technique, loss-focused attention, holds significant potential for further investigation. It seeks to improve model performance by incorporating specific loss-related modifications. We intend to further examine the benefits and limitations of this approach and explore its potential for improving the accuracy of models like the one we developed. Ultimately, our goal is to identify and investigate innovative methods for understanding and improving the accuracy of these models, which are crucial tools for infrequently updated AI systems responsible for classifying hate speech across various platforms. Such techniques could ultimately contribute to the seamless integration of these models into more efficient and effective AI systems. We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that capture the overall dynamics of these networks. By assuming random connections, we analyze the effects of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on synaptically and gap junction coupled networks. Our findings reveal that the out-degree distribution has no impact on synaptically coupled network dynamics. Broadening the in-degree distribution of inhibitory networks eliminates oscillations and narrows the bistability range in excitatory networks. Conversely, in gap junction coupled networks, in-degree distribution variations shift the onset points for collective oscillations. Many of these results persist in networks of more biologically accurate neurons. Our work highlights the importance of considering neuronal network connectivity when designing therapies for neurological conditions. The insights gained here can also be applied to larger networks of more intricate neurons, providing valuable guidance for modeling and simulation efforts in neuroscience. The findings have the potential to extend to other types of neurons, including those with dynamic degree of excitability. Furthermore, these results may be relevant not only to theta neurons but also to a broader class of neurons known as integrate and fire neurons with adaptive refractory periods. various methods being explored. One area of research focuses on search-based approaches,
using semantic-rich abstract syntax tree representations to guide a search for potential fixes.
We have found that generating an effective search space can be challenging, particularly when
focusing on fix generation for an individual input, as other feasible solutions may exist.
Our innovative method utilizes an adversarial patch technique, generated by an adversary working
against a syntax tree parser, to overcome this limitation. An adversary seeks to produce a patch
that, when combined with a syntax tree, results in a different parsed tree.
We have successfully applied this technique to two search-based APR platforms: the JMerger platform
for merging parallel function implementations, and the JPatch platform for fix generation.
Our empirical results demonstrate that our approach yields significantly higher repair rates and
better repair accuracy compared to traditional methods. Moreover, our technique appears to be
generalizable to other APR techniques beyond search-based repair methods. 
It can potentially be used to improve other APR methods as well. 
For example, generating an adversarial patch for JSON data reveals weaknesses in JSON parsers,
exposing previously unknown vulnerabilities. 
An attacker could exploit these vulnerabilities to launch successful AP attacks on JSON-based systems.
Consequently, our presented technique has significant implications for both the APR and AP research
and may also have practical applications in testing software systems for robustness and security. 
Moreover, our technique is simple to use and requires no significant changes to existing APR code.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, effectively preserving their components across orthogonal dimensions. This 'randomized sketching' approach has numerous applications across various data sciences and machine learning domains. The resilience of CountSketch to'malicious' or 'oblivious' adaptive inputs has been studied in existing literature; however, a significant gap remains in understanding its robustness when faced with a combination of these threats. This paper addresses this gap by providing the first study on the resilience of CountSketch to adaptive inputs, characterizing its behavior in terms of worst-case guarantees. Specifically, we demonstrate that CountSketch resists severe attacks under certain conditions but cannot do so under others, no matter how large the involved parameters are. We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to $n$ buyers with unit demand, where each buyer buys one item and has private valuations for the items. The goal is to maximize the mechanism's revenue. The revenue generated is defined as the price paid for each item multiplied by its quantity sold. The price of an item is equal to the maximum of the minimum prices set by the seller for that item and the prices reported by buyers. A robust triangle inequality is applied to determine the prices reported by buyers. The feasibility of achieving a revenue guarantee was previously studied under a specific pricing range, while this study considers an open pricing range. Theoretical results show that any revenue-maximizing mechanism must either be an auction or a specific type of auction. A variant of the VCG auction auction is proposed, which is shown to be the first mechanism with a revenue guarantee for this problem within an absolute error. The performance of the proposed auction is evaluated in scenarios where buyers either have independent valuations or a single common valuation. The common valuation scenario is used to determine a specific revenue guarantee for this problem, while independent valuations are used to compare the performance of various pricing mechanisms to a certain upper bound on revenue. This paper aims to fill the gap by establishing a semantic framework for quantum control within the unitary sphere using control points as inputs and output states. The study centers on λS1, a lambda calculus that represents quantum control, and its corresponding categorical model. In the context of glaciology, particularly when modelling contact-related issues in marine ice sheets, Stokes variational inequalities come into play. This research focuses on a specific inequality involving a pre-strain term, stemming from the balance between ice pressure and friction. We introduce a family of finite element approximations for this model, utilizing standard conforming approximations for the velocity and weakly conforming schemes for the stress tensor. We achieve these approximations while handling potential non-conformity issues and high-order complications. A key challenge lies in proving the existence and uniqueness of the approximate solutions, due to the absence of suffcient stability and maximum principles for the stress tensor. By leveraging a semiconductor regularization approach, we establish these principles in the approximate setting. Under reasonable regularity assumptions, we derive error estimates for the approximate solutions, drawing inspiration from classical Stokes error estimates. This work culminates in the proof of a unique finite element approximation for the entire Stokes variational inequality. Finally, through the $L^2$-projected rotated quads method, we obtain optimal error estimates for the approximate stress tensor in the entire domain, drawing upon the work of of Krouglikov and Petrov. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it on the target dataset. Top methodologies for pre-training
involve either using multi-layer perceptron predictions of pixel colors or
segmenting image regions. Recently, depth estimation from monocular images has
gained traction, suggesting it could provide benefits for segmentation tasks. 
This study aims to uncover whether depth estimation pre-training is superior to
the prevailing techniques of color and image segmentation for driving segmentation
model training. Although prior research indicates that depth and segmentation
are correlated, our analysis shows that using a monocular depth estimation
approach for pre-training introduces inaccuracies, particularly on complex
datasets. We propose that using monocular depth estimates as color maps could be
beneficial, however this remains unverified in our study. Ultimately, our study
concludes that simple image segmentation with a basic UNet architecture is the
most effective pre-training strategy for driving segmentation models, while the
value of more intricate techniques and deep neural networks for pre-training has
not been clearly established. 
The study presents new methods for evaluating segmentation accuracy when there
are inconsistencies between predicted and target labels. We also provide a
benchmark for assessing the impact of pre-training on segmentation models, and
make available our source code and datasets for others to use. 
The research was performed on the Cityscapes and KITTI57 datasets, and our study
shows that simple segmentation with a UNet architecture significantly outperforms
pre-training with a more complex PWC-Net, and is comparable to or even better
than pre-training with a colour encoder. 
Our study suggests that while more sophisticated pre-training methods may be
beneficial under specific conditions, a basic UNet for pre-training is a good
choice.

It is evident that deep neural networks excel in predictive tasks, yet they require substantial and high-quality labeled data for optimal performance. In cases where such data is scarce or unavailable, it often proves impractical or financially burdensome to acquire. To mitigate this challenge, researchers have developed innovative solutions to overcome the gap between a network's training and testing environments. These solutions, known as deep neural network domain adaptation techniques, aim to minimize the network's sensitivity to domain differences to enhance generalization. This work evaluates six prominent deep neural network domain adaptation techniques, including self-learning methods, supervised learning methods, and semi-supervised learning methods, using image classification tasks. To facilitate a comprehensive understanding, we compared the algorithms under three distinct scenarios: with comprehensive knowledge of the testing domain, with limited testing data, and with an abundance of unlabeled testing data. To ensure objectivity, we employed a standardized evaluation process, including a unified codebase for a fair assessment. Our results, represented by accuracy or error rate values, demonstrated that certain domain adaptation techniques outperformed others, depending on the data and a priori domain knowledge availability. To facilitate a thorough discussion, we provided a domain adaptation taxonomy and definitions of key technical terms. Contrary to the prevailing belief that graph neural networks are inherently transparent, current explainer methods are often hindered by impractically high computational costs when applied to real-world scenarios. To effectively address this issue, we developed an innovative explainer, Weighted SubGraph Sampler (WSGS), which produces an interpretable breakdown of the learned model into a set of influential subgraphs. This method efficiently captures the key factors driving model predictions within a weighty Graph Neural Network, thus yielding transparent and understandable results. Thorough experiments conducted across multiple datasets and scenarios validate the efficacy of WSGS, as demonstrated by its superior performance in Explaining (predicting from interpretable subgraphs) and Local Explaining (with limited context) scenarios. Moreover, by integrating WSGS with the recent sample-efficient technique, Edge Embedding, we successfully apply it to real-world scenarios involving thousands of nodes and demonstrate its capability to accurately extract 95% of the knowledge embedded in the trained model. Consequently, the developed WSGS algorithm presents a novel and practical solution to understanding Graph Neural Networks. By leveraging this method, researchers and practitioners are empowered to conduct in-depth analyses of the learned models, thereby fostering additional research opportunities. For example, we can systematically analyze the relative importance of the model's built-in components (e.g., different layers, neurons, and connections) and identify which components are contributing significantly to the model's performance. This, in turn, enables us to refine and optimize the neural network architecture and design by pinpointing which components to adjust. As such, the proposed WSGS algorithm serves as a versatile and efficient tool for grasping the intricate workings of Graph Neural Networks. Our study is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/leeom/Weighted-SubGraph-Sampler. The experimental results were obtained using https://github.com/leeom/Edge-Targeted-Neural-Network-Pruning. The obtained insights are expected to contribute significantly to the further development of transparent and efficient graph neural networks. Moreover, the revealed knowledge is anticipated to foster the creation of open-source, parameterized explainer libraries, thereby bridging the existing gap and facilitating the creation of understandable, context-specific models capable of accurate inference. We examine a two-wave system, each wave traveling through different dimensions, and analyze its stability using the energy method. This system includes a visco-elastic structure that absorbs energy with a Kelvin-Voigt model, with a nonlinear damping factor that behaves differently at different distances from the origin. We prove that the initial conditions and boundary conditions, affected by external forces, cause the system to become unstable after a certain period, provided there are specific resonance relationships between the frequencies and frequencies of the initial conditions and boundary conditions. This resonance ensures that the energy of the system decreases over time, causing instability. Conversely, we prove that the absence of such resonance relationships, combined with certain conditions on the behavior of the external forces, results in the energy of the system decreasing exponentially over time, causing energy absorption and stability, using the finite energy method. This research extends previous studies on the stability of coupled wave equations to a more complex model, with nonlinear damping and initially moving boundary conditions, and establishes the conditions under which the system becomes unstable or stable. We further investigate a model with nonlinear damping that exhibits completely different behavior at different distances from the origin, and prove that, unlike the case with a visco-elastic structure, the system is always unstable, with a growing energy at a certain rate, regardless of the frequencies and positions of the initial conditions and boundary conditions. This research was motivated by a model of a membrane inside a bell, with a three-dimensional outside and two-dimensional inside, and analyzes its behavior using both approaches to demonstrate that the outside membrane can cause the inside membrane to become unstable, while the inside membrane can cause the outside membrane to become unstable due to resonance, and that the growth of the energy of the inside membrane is a maximum when it is near the resonance frequency and the outside membrane is at rest. This result provides an explanation for why a broken glass is often heard after the inside membrane has become unstable. This research was supported by the research fund of Konkuk University. To address this issue, research has developed kernel mixture models that categorize the blurring effect into distinct groups, allowing for the estimation of a latent image. The model has been tested using the IMDB dataset with promising results that surpass state-of-the-art deblurring methods. The source code for the algorithm can be accessed at the link: https://github.com/keivanB/Blind-Image-Deblurring-Based-on-Kernel-Mixture. The model has also been tested in an experiment where the algorithm's performance on noiseless images was compared to the performance of state-of-the-art methods on the IMDB dataset. The model's results show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of the overall sharpness of the estimated images and their similarity to the ground truth. Furthermore, we establish equivalent definitions of covariant BiHom-bialgebra with quasitriangular properties and show that the BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation of weight -1 can be derived from a coassociative cooperative BiHom-bialgebra. Lastly, we outline two methods for constructing BiHom-pre-Lie modules from Rota-Baxter paired modules and R-symmetric BiHom-algebras, respectively. Additionally, we investigate NAD-BiHom-algebras within the context of BiHom-Yang-Baxter equations of weight 1. The main content of this research is to solve the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system through the use of BiHom-Yang-Baxter pairs with weight 1. Specifically, we show that the curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-algebra can be redefined as a precolor BiHom-algebra, and precolor actions can provide a solution to the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system when the weight of the BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair is 1. Moreover, when the weight of the BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair is 1, we are able to establish a connection between matched groupoids and the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system. The curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-algebra can also be redefined as a matched module within the context of a matched groupoid. The solutions to the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system are generated by the Twisted Yang-Baxter equation, which is derived from the given BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation. Formal verification offers precise guarantees for software with critical implications.  However, writing specifications in a formal language accessible to natural language speakers is a highly complex and time-consuming task.  On the other hand, specifications based on logical forms are more straightforward, yet limited by the capacity to express these forms, which is currently a subject of research.  This paper presents Hoare logic for a logic programming language, extended with imprecision handling, and demonstrates a translation from specifications in logical forms to this language.  This translation enables us to leverage well-developed verification tools, providing a crucial link between compositional and model-checking-based verification.  This paper includes model-checking-based verification tool applications to programs derived from algorithms expressed in pseudocode, using a language with arrays and heap data storage.  Specifically, we consider algorithms for searching a list, algorithmic selection, and data reconstruction.  Although the translation process is semi-automatic, we outline potential methods for full automation, including semantic analysis of logical forms.  This study marks an initial development towards utilizing advanced language processing techniques to bridge the specification writing gap between natural language and a formal language.  It establishes a promising specification writing link, yet highlights certain obstacles within the model transformation process.  Future advancements in specification reading will further minimize this gap.  This study was conducted as part of the Resourceful Language project.  All used resources, including project-related materials, are publicly accessible through https://resourcefullang.github.io/nhl/.  An implementation of the developed tools is also available at https://github.com/vstheoring/nhl.  An executable version of the developed tools, as well as the related research, can be found at https://dl.sf.net. Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within the network. The existing Canopus protocol excels at performance, however, struggles when dealing with failures that don't directly affect performance, leading to the development of RCanopus. RCanopus enhances Canopus to not only tolerate various types of failures but also to guarantee the accurate detection and recovery of failures and protect against malicious attacks, all while maintaining agreement among live nodes. Through a combination of failure-tolerant design and an innovative failure detection and recovery mechanism, RCanopus achieves this without introducing an additional leader, thus ensuring consensus performance remains efficient, with specific aspects of the algorithm confirmed using formal verification tools. Experimental evaluations of RCanopus validate its ability to effectively operate under different failure scenarios while maintaining a high level of performance, even in the event of multiple failures occurring. Further analysis reveals that RCanopus outperforms other fault-tolerant consensus algorithms in both performance and resource usage.
