This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. VMOA_p can be understood as the closure of the analytic functions within VMOA in the compact-open topology. Our focus lies in characterizing the maximal ideals and exploring the topological properties of the spaces. We have also derived the criteria under which the semigroup of composition operators is continuous or compact when acting on BMOA_p and VMOA_p. A semitopological differential structure is established on the maximal ideal space, leading to the definition of the hyperstonean compactification of the unit disk. Our research further extends to developing boundedness criteria for integral operators in BMOA and VMOA. An operator T is said to be integral if it can be expressed as T(f)(z) = (bf)(z) + ∫∞ zero f(z)g(z,ξ)dξ for some function b and a measure dξ on the unit circle. The study determines the necessary and sufficient conditions under which T is bounded when acting on BMOA and VMOA. We have also derived the relationship between Carleson measures for BMOA and VMOA. Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model often requires identifying key features of its conformal field theory, particularly the structure of primary operators and operator product expansion. A recent approach proposed by C\'eleghini and Viola involves using wavefunction overlaps to derive operator fusion and related properties. We have employed this method in studies of the Haagerup model, a quantum spin chain whose conformal field theory properties have been unclear. From wavefunction overlaps, we were able to determine the operator product expansion, identify primary operators, and conformal dimensions, as well as calculate universal finite-size correction terms and critical energies. Additionally, low-lying excited states were used to confirm the expected operator product expansion and scaling dimensions. The obtained results match previously published data, providing a standalone validation of the approach. We have also extended this method to a universal coset conformal field theory, Type I$_p$, and derived scaling dimensions and operator product expansions for $p=3,4,5,6$. The results obtained from wavefunction overlaps match known conformal field theory properties. We were able to determine the operator product expansions and scaling dimensions for all studied models without relying on prior knowledge of the conformal field theory. The approach is generally applicable and can be used to study other models whose conformal field theories are not yet fully understood. It can also be employed to study non-intertwined multi-component spin one chains, a class of models similar to the XXZ chain. However, in models with conformal field theory properties that have previously been extensively analyzed, the approach may not reveal significantly new information. It may also be limited by numerical precision in large finite-size correction calculations. We have addressed these limitations by applying the method to the Haagerup model and Type I$_p$ conformal field theories. We provide a standalone validation of the approach by matching known conformal field theory properties with results obtained from wavefunction overlaps. We also propose future studies, including extending the approach to XXZ spin one chain and the higher-leg spin Kitaev model. We anticipate that the method will be widely applicable in the near future to study other models whose conformal field theory properties are not yet fully understood. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task in linguistic research, typically addressed through machine learning algorithms that assign a single POS tag to each sentence element. However, POS tagging historical texts presents unique challenges, primarily attributed to limited accuracy in the POS tagger and potential errors in the input text. To enhance the reliability of POS tagging historical texts, we introduce a novel approach based on set-valued prediction, aiming to provide a comprehensive set of plausible POS tags for each sentence element. By acknowledging the potential for errors in both the POS tagger and the input text, the proposed set-valued prediction offers a reliable range of possible tags, thus rectifying incorrect annotations caused by tagging errors or text inaccuracies, ultimately resulting in more accurate POS-tagged historical corpora. To demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, we successfully applied set-valued prediction to two French corpora: the ARTEL collection containing modernization texts from the 19th century, and the CORPES II collection spanning a period from 14th to 19th centuries. By utilizing the deep neural network-based set-valued predictor developed by von Mengershausen et al. (2021), we observed a notable increase in the accuracy of POS tags for the modernization texts of the ARTEL collection, averaging 17.9% above the single-valued predictor. Furthermore, our approach also identified substantial errors in the annotated CORPES II collection, highlighting its potential for optimal results on larger collections like ARTEL. The results of our research indicate that the proposed set-valued prediction method is an indispensable tool for enhancing the reliability of POS tagging historical texts. Additionally, to facilitate the creation of high-quality annotated historical collections, we provide access to both the source code and the pre-trained models for the ARTEL collection on the ADRAS platform at: https://adras-platform.org/resources/arete/corpus/arete-corpus.html#tagging-errors. This paper's primary goal is to develop a conceptual framework for addressing challenges in variational analysis, with a focus on extending Karlin's integrability concept to the context of nonsmooth functions. The investigation includes examining the relationship between this idea and the more specific property of lower-DC (lower separable in certain variables) functions, as defined by the Kontchakovski-Dubovitskii decomposition. The results presented demonstrate that every nonsmooth lower-DC multi-function can be expressed as a complementarity of two contrasting functions, with one function exhibiting better regularity than the other. The evidence and theory underpinning this conclusion involve multiple forms of complementarity, including that based on the basic variable. The research also includes examples designed to illustrate key distinctions between various forms of complementarity as well as a proof that iteratively applying a particular reparameterization procedure always results in a complementarity of contrasting regularities. The implications of this finding are that every nonsmooth lower-DC multi-function is inherently iteratively parameterizable in the same category of complementarity. The developed theory has a range of applications spanning from fixed-point and equilibrium theory to parametric optimization and equilibrium theory, with an accompanying model-based analysis illustrating the potential practical uses of this research. The results presented can be seen as a comprehensive extension and generalization of Karlin's findings to the context of nonsmooth functions. The associated theoretical validation of fixed-point and equilibrium theories for parametrically defined multi-functions with the lower-DC property highlights the significant practical value of this research in the study of variational analysis. The resulting theory represents an important contribution to the field of nonsmooth analysis, with a considerable, heretofore unaddressed differential aspect that distinguishes this research from the work of others. The accompanying model-based analysis serves to illustrate the substantial, concrete applications of this research in the study of variational analysis. The results presented are anticipated to be instrumental in the formulation of innovative, regularity-based concepts of multi-functions in the context of nonsmooth analysis. The evidence and theory presented in this research indicate that iterative procedures hold the key to identifying and characterizing critical properties of nonsmooth functions. The resulting theory is a substantial, heretofore unaddressed contribution to the field of nonsmooth analysis, with the potential to positively impact a wide range of areas within variational analysis. The evidence and theory presented in this research are novel and significant, with the potential to establish a foundation for novel regularity results for nonsmooth functions

As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, machine-readable specifications. Nevertheless, human requirements often lack essential information, or they contain inaccuracies or ambiguities stemming from written English text. We introduce CitySpec, an innovative AI-powered system for formalizing smart city needs, which effectively bridges language gaps and resolves common data inconsistencies. The purpose of this research is to explain CitySpec's functionality by showcasing three practical applications: real-time requirements completion within CitySpec; a collaborative correction process when unexpected exceptions occur; and the adaptive learning mechanism of CitySpec. By demonstrating these capabilities through tangible examples, we demonstrate CitySpec's effectiveness in efficiently guiding non-technical smart city officials in converting requirements into usable specifications. The learning capability of CitySpec significantly reduces the overall specification creation time, as its officials require fewer guidance requests over time. The substantial user savings in time result directly from CitySpec's dynamic learning capacity. Additionally, CitySpec's ability to address unexpected exceptions enhances its reliability in producing accurate specifications, and this is achieved at a significantly faster rate compared to previous solutions. The adapted version of CitySpec displayed comparable efficiency in generating specifications, but with the added benefit of increased reliability. A joint adaptive learning mechanism was also tested on other smart city requirements platforms and specifications, yielding similar outcomes, and further research is recommended to expand on these results. The original version of this research was published in Science of Science and Technology of Modern Computer Systems in 2020. The research presented here represents a refined and extended version of that initial work.

In the category of sets, the best partial order approximation of the image in such a case is obtained by forming the cofibered image of the original preorder above the epimorphism. In categories satisfying regularity conditions, the existence of such a cofibered image of a partial order corresponds to the existence of the least upper bound among all partial orders within the category. Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of more than 300 kilometers, along with a substantial decrease in location-specific extreme weather dependence. This reveals that locations more exposed to severe storms, such as offshore oil platforms, experience significantly higher extreme weather frequencies beyond 300 kilometers, in contrast to coastal areas which show notably lower frequencies beyond 300 kilometers compared to historical forecasts. However, locations closer to each other, like oil platforms near the coast, continue to exhibit substantial extreme weather dependence. This study highlights the importance of conditional models in understanding and quantifying the patterns of severe storms in diverse environments. By using these models, accurate estimates of severe storm frequencies can be achieved, allowing policymakers to assess the impact of severe storms on critical offshore structures such as oil platforms, resulting in better risk management decisions. Several key model limitations were identified during the study, including irregular spatial patterns in severe storms, variability in wind speed and wave measurements, and changes in the average frequency of severe storms over time, all of which could potentially be addressed by expanding the model. Expanding the model involves incorporating additional data types, such as in situ measurements, and using integrated multi-data approaches to account for the average frequency of severe storms over time. Expanding the model also allows the incorporation of irregular spatial patterns through stochastic models and reduces model limitations by using alternative transformations of wind speed and wave measurements. Future research plans to address these limitations by developing improved models. 
Data for this study can be accessed through several sources, including the Metop satellite website and the EMODnet Biogeoographical Atlas, with the analysis conducted using the R statistical environment, incorporating 12 supplementary materials. 
Using this study's results, recommendations for improved forecasting and mitigation strategies are proposed, including changes to the placement of offshore structures and enhanced risk management across the region. 
This research highlights the value of collaborative efforts between the weather and energy industries in addressing the complex challenges of severe storms and extreme weather conditions.

To enhance the accuracy of computational models plagued by noisy data and parameters, this study addresses the issue of reducing error in a linear system affected by uncertainty. By building upon Etter and Ying's '20 foundational work, which demonstrated the feasibility of shifting operators to mitigate error in linear system noise, this research expands that capability to non-diagonal matrices. This extension is complicated by the larger size and complexity of the transfer function resulting from the matrix differentiation, distinguishing it from the more tractable diagonal matrix case. In response to this challenge, this study introduces the concept of "within-method" convergence, a computationally relaxed condition facilitating the analysis of this more complex scenario. This study presents a theoretical framework, outlining a class of methods capable of decreasing error in matrices. Additionally, some methods proposed here provide error reduction guarantees. To further illustrate the utility of these concepts, some experimental results demonstrating within-method convergence are presented. In experiments involving sparse CCSM systems, a method proposed here significantly reduces error compared to traditional approaches, demonstrating up to a 60% improvement. This study's methods and findings have real-world implications, translating to computational savings of up to 43% in a CCSM model used in the simulation of a molecular qubit. Our work is implemented in the open-source library noisyop, which is accompanied by an open-source repository containing the code used in this study, along with a fully implemented CCSM model for quantum systems. The application of machine learning in image diagnostics is rapidly gaining clinical traction, yet faces hurdles in the clinical setting due to inconsistencies in annotation format. Standardization is widely recognized as the key to integrating ML technology into routine pathology and radiology practice, but current solutions often fall short. Many attempts to standardize through formal processes, like DICOM and IHE, come with significant implementation hurdles. Highdicom aims to bridge this gap by providing a set of 35 Python tools that facilitate the conversion and interpretation of standardized DICOM and IHE images, allowing for greater flexibility in the clinical workflow. These tools, developed specifically for the needs of the medical imaging community, are available under a permissive open-source license, making it easier for researchers and clinicians to adopt them. We detail our implementation challenges and the resulting tools, specifically designed to address problems at each stage of the ML pipeline, from data preparation to model output and validation. We demonstrate their effectiveness in a variety of practical applications. Our solutions address problems associated with reading and writing DICOM files, standardizing ML model outputs, converting CSV and JSON to DICOM, and clustering such that it's compatible with DICOM. Many of these tools performed per-image classification or regression operations per pixel, providing model interpretable output in terms of original and modified image features in DICOM format. We provide example code to facilitate per-pixel classification using a Keras model. Our open-source project, Highdicom, is available under a very permissive public domain dedication, allowing for widespread adoption without the need for licensing agreements. We discuss the implications of adopting standardization formats in practice and how Highdicom can facilitate this process, ultimately contributing to the integration of ML technology into the clinical setting. We also provide a freely available Python 3.6+ image analysis container, built on Docker, to facilitate the deployment of ML models in clinical settings. This container includes the tools developed during our research, as well as pre-trained models for common tasks, making it permissive, shareable, and per-image diagnostics-friendly. Importing highdicom or starting the corresponding Docker container container provides researchers and clinicians with a wide array of established tools, ultimately facilitating the standardization of ML model outputs. By providing a suite of tools, facilitating standardization in image diagnostics, we have taken a crucial step forward in the clinical adoption of ML technology. Highdicom is available at https://pypi.org/project/highdicom/ and the Docker container is available at https://doi.org/10.6092/medicine/202

Pearson's product moment correlation coefficient (PMC) is often used to compare connections 
between two datasets. However, this correlation coefficient can be unreliable when calculating 
its value due to its sensitivity to extreme data points. A more reliable alternative, the sample 
spearmans rank correlation coefficient (SSRRC), offers some immunity to data distortions. 
Despite this, calculating SSRRC can be laborious and consuming time and effort. This study 
demonstrates that using SSRRC to estimate PMC yields predictable outcomes when dealing with 
various data sets, suggesting that SSRRC can be an effective way to predict PMC's reliability. 
A function was developed to determine the predictable probability distribution of SSRRC's 
sample moments as data sets change order. This distribution was derived from treating each data 
set as an ordered sequence. Through an ordered data approach, the probability distribution of 
SSRRC sample moments was developed and found to be consistent with known characteristics. 
Additionally, the probability distribution of PMC sample moments was developed and found 
to be consistent with theoretical estimates. Employing these probability distributions 
approximately replicates key characteristics of their underlying distributions. Finally, the new 
probability distributions were verified using simulations with diverse data sets.

sets based on their shapes and central location. This approach was then used to compare and

combination of techniques, data correction, re-ranking, and re-ordering, yields the most 
effective outcome in improving statistical estimates. Ultimately, the proposed methods can 
significantly improve parameter and relationship estimates in statistics.

Language learning dictionaries can facilitate vocabulary acquisition by supplying 
word definitions, although conventional dictionaries may struggle with 
capturing word meanings that vary across specific contexts. A potential solution 
is to create an electronic dictionary that provides user-generated definitions and
establishes an online community where terms and their meanings can be submitted 
and reviewed by others. This community-driven approach enables more nuanced 
definitions and allows users to discover terms related to their interests, thus
making user-generated online dictionaries a promising tool for language learning. 
This paper presents LitMind Dictionary, an open-source user-generated dictionary 
designed to aid English learners in their vocabulary development. As a result of 
COVID-19, the number of users on LitMind Dictionary has significantly increased, 
leading to a substantial expansion of its term collection from 500,000 to over 2 
million terms. Research has been conducted to compare LitMind Dictionary with 
traditional dictionaries like Oxford Dictionary and Cambridge Dictionary, with 
results indicating LitMind Dictionary's superior performance in aiding user 
vocabularies. Moreover, an analysis of user behavior and content on LitMind 
Dictionary has provided valuable insights for improving the dictionary's content and 
user experience. Ultimately, the paper highlights the potential benefits of 
community-driven language learning tools like LitMind Dictionary for language

Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate-based post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent reliability, especially in critical applications such as human-centric recommendation tasks. Moreover, an ideal explanation should enhance trust in users, however, current explanations often provide unreliable insights into how recommendations were generated. For instance, an explanation might suggest one product over another, yet still indicate another product as highly relevant. In response to these limitations, we present the concept of "adherence" to clarify the relationship between an explanation and the user's actual preferences. Furthermore, we propose the "adherence and constancy" criterion to assess the reliability of post-hoc explanations in relation to both recommendation accuracy and user perception. Experimental findings based on actual user preferences and human evaluations reveal a significant drop-off in the quality of several leading post-hoc explanation methods meeting this criterion. Interestingly, an analysis of the results suggests that enhancing "constancy" is key to addressing this issue, and we propose an adaptation of the LIME method, named LIME-RS, capable of generating more reliable explanations. Positioning these quantum wells extremely close to the surface of the semiconductor material causes a notable shift in the energy levels located very close to the surface in comparison to deeper levels. In order to study Fermi level pinning in near-surface InAs quantum wells, researchers used photoemission spectroscopy on well-developed InAs(111)/GaAs surfaces that had undergone various growth conditions. The results revealed that increasing the InAs growth, as well as the thickness of the GaAs layer, caused a notable increase in the binding energy of the QW and a notable decrease in the energy gap between the two main energy levels. Furthermore, researchers were able to determine that surface states located at 1.2 eV above the vacuum level were responsible for levels pinning, while results also suggested that composition and morphology played significant roles in the overall phenomenon, ultimately allowing researchers to control Fermi level pinning in near-surface InAs quantum wells. In order to further study near-surface InAs quantum wells, researchers were able to position the Fermi level of a 6.5 nm quantum well 0.28 eV below the energy level of the conduction edge, while positioning the valence maxima 0.30 eV above the energy level of the Fermi level. This issue is addressed in a newly proposed statistical framework for the nearest neighbor classification method, which handles datasets where the majority classes outweigh minority ones. Initially developed for binary classification problems, this method is extended to accommodate multiple classes. Unlike existing over-sampling techniques that involve generating fake data points, this method achieves replicable results by sidestepping pseudo observation generation. Moreover, this method has demonstrated Bayesian risk consistency when subjected to relevant conditions and shows significant improvement in its performance compared to other existing methods, all backed up by a comprehensive analysis of several reference datasets. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech. Moreover, the median-based output strategy results in higher accuracy when predicting the mean duration, outperforming other generation methods. Ultimately, this new duration modelling method integrates seamlessly with a state-of-the-art synthesis system, improving its performance. The associated code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/jjwrig/median-based_duration_modeling. Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots cannot consistently meet the required flatness condition, which is necessary to ensure precise and accurate motion. This research introduces a novel controller for an N-degree-of-freedom industrial robot that uses supplementary sensors to compensate for its inherent elasticity. The proposed controller leverages a recursive algorithm to compute a flatness-based motion profile, and is supported by a supplementary feedback control that adjusts real-time motion dynamics. The study validates the effectiveness of this controller through both theoretical and experimental assessments, demonstrating its ability to ensure flatness and achieve fast, high-quality motion. A key benefit of this controller is its simplicity, requiring only the integration of a single linear regulator and the application of a flatness-based motion profile, and can be easily implemented using existing position feedback from the robot joints. The experimental results demonstrate that this controller is capable of producing fast and precise motions, with an average position error of less than 0.05 mm and a average orientation error of less than 0.02 degrees. Furthermore, the results indicate that this controller can enable high-speed motion, with an average velocity of up to 3 m/s. This controller has the potential to significantly enhance the capabilities of existing industrial robots by compensating for their inherent elasticity and ensuring flatness, even in complex applications such as milling and grinding. Due to its simplicity, this controller can be easily adopted by manufacturers and users, and is compatible with a wide range of industrial robots as well as various elasticity models and flatness-based motion planning methods. In addition to its widespread applicability, the controller's properties can be easily analyzed and understood through the computation of a transfer matrix, which is used to determine the flatness-based motion profile. By addressing the key challenges facing the adoption of advanced motion planning methods in the industry, the resulting findings aim to ensure that industrial robots and equipment are used to their full potential. One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly over distance. This method employs overlapping grids at each atomic site, effectively dividing the integrand. Although the unaltered Becke scheme exhibits slow convergence when applied to free electronic states found in processes like photoionization, this modified version achieves efficient results comparable to those for bound states. To attain the same level of precision as the modified scheme for bound states, the original Becke scheme requires significantly smaller error tolerances. To handle non-overlapping quadrature methods where integrals are evaluated using multiple atomic sites, we developed an additional algorithm based on construction schemes first proposed by Becke and Trefilov. This new algorithm successfully generalizes the modified scheme's concepts for use in schemes with no overlap. We have thoroughly tested our methods' convergence properties for various functions with different decay patterns in one and two dimensions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that our algorithms can be effectively used in parallel to evaluate integrals in complex systems such as the hydrogen dimer and bulk hydrogen. All of our code for these new algorithms is freely available under the open-source GNU Public License. Additionally, we have generated a variety of pre-compiled libraries, dubbed libmole, which are freely available for use. These libraries are compatible with a wide range of compilers and allow the user to evaluate integrals designed for various numerical schemes. We have also provided documentation for the codes and libraries using the Doxygen system, making it easy to use the methods and code developed. Finally, we have demonstrated that our algorithms can be effectively used in a new implementation of the quantum Monte Carlo method, known as turbomole-PIMSC. Using this approach, we were able to calculate an accurate value for the hydrogen dissociation energy, a well-established benchmark in the field. The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class examples, and its two variants along with random oversampling in text classification tasks. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its Borderline and ADASYN modifications, and random oversampling in text classification using text from news sources, a challenging area due to its multi-class nature, and evaluates their efficiency using two datasets, Cohn-Marsh and Reuters-8. The study compares the performance of these oversampling methods with and without ensemble voting using support vector machines and k-nearest neighbors algorithms. The research finds that random oversampling and SMOTE perform equally well in two-class topics, but random oversampling outperforms SMOTE in multi-class topics. Additionally, the study discovers that using ensemble voting enhances the overall performance of oversampling methods, and random oversampling outperforms SMOTE and its modifications in text classification tasks. The research also finds that multi-class topics receive higher text classification accuracy compared to two-class topics, and ensemble voting further improves the already strong performance of random oversampling methods in multi-class topics. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses an inherent systematics tied to its conservation laws, with the angular momentum conservation law being particularly susceptible to inaccuracies due to weak and strong boundary conditions. This vulnerability is not only present in direct sum approaches but also affects methods such as the fast multipole method and kernel independent particle methods. However, some implementations are able to minimize this error. In this study, the reason behind this inaccuracies will be identified and corrected in the Fourier and adapted fast multipole algorithms. We will also examine the impact of this error on the stability and accuracy of the simulations and provide numerical evidence to support this assertion. Numerical results indicate that accurate angular momentum conservation does not necessarily translate to a stable solution, as stable solutions can still exhibit conservation violations and vice versa. We will provide the Fourier and FM methods with the conservation properties of SPH, a crucial step in verifying SPH code quality. We anticipate this research will set a new standard for validating FM and Fourier implementations. Code supporting this research is publicly available on the Bitbucket repository https://bitbucket.org/irishsph codes. We address the issue of efficiently learning from experienced teachers. Although prior research has focused on learning from teachers that provide perfect, yet unknown feedback, our study instead focuses on learning from imperfect teachers. In the context of learning to play Atari games, for instance, our model utilizes feedback from a parametric expert that may not always be correct. By incorporating a generator network to create diverse examples of game states, our approach enables students to learn indirectly from these imperfect teachers, thereby discovering correct actions by exploring different perspectives on the teachers' policies. We implement a variant of the famous VDN model using our data augmentation framework and demonstrate the effectiveness of the combination in a range of experiments, resulting in performance superior to that achieved by models that learn directly from the teachers or through self-supervised learning alone. Moreover, our data augmentation framework is shown to be versatile, being applicable to various other learning settings, such as multi-agent induction, as well as to learn multiple policies as diverse strategies for a single task in a curriculum learning setting. These results collectively suggest that our data augmentation framework is a powerful tool for efficient learning from experienced teachers. A comprehensive study of the creation of two Higgs bosons ($hh$) paired with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) using a massive dataset of 139 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy has been carried out utilizing the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The research explores final states in which the vector boson decays into electrons or muons and the $hh$ pair into two or four b-quarks. No signs of $hh$ production have been detected thus far, and expected upper limits under various theories, including both the Standard Model and the Standard Model with moderate strong interaction contributions, have been determined. The limits set a 95% confidence upper bound of 83 to 203 times the Standard Model's predicted rate for the $WWhh$ or $ZZhh$ signatures, or 83 to 439 times for the $WW($4$b$) signature. This research aims to further refine the understanding of the Higgs sector's nature. The investigation into the $WW($4$b$) signature presents an entirely new endeavor. The findings have also been interpreted using theoretical models of composite Higgs bosons and fuzzy dark matter. For the first time, the research has provided constraints on the triviality bounds for the composite Higgs models for the $ZZ($4$b$) signature. The research has also established strict limits on the production of supersymmetric particles in supersymmetric models incorporating moderate mixing between Higgs bosons and supersymmetric particles. The research has also provided the most sensitive and extensive examination of the Higgs boson's interaction with itself, specifically the interaction's strength and direction, in any previously observed phenomenon. By combining the research's results, the interaction's strength has been constrained to be less than 12 times the Standard Model's predicted value with 95% confidence. Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation demonstrate enhanced sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities.
This technology, in conjunction with phase-coherent feedback from detected signals to modulation, enables the creation of a resonant spin maser system highly sensitive to changes in background magnetic fields.
Our system incorporates digital signal processing integrated into the maser feedback loop to optimize its performance.
Using a 40K atomic magnetometer built with low-cost, commercially available components and driven by a single board computer, we have measured the gold standard's magnetic field variability, ISO 3109, with results comparable to those obtained with more sophisticated equipment.
Our results show that digital spin masers can be highly effective in monitoring environmental magnetic fields.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers through the identification and computation of relevant algebraic numbers derived from Lefschetz-type formulas and their corresponding residues. These calculations involve explicit estimates based on Lefschetz-type formulas, yielding a comprehensive analysis. Notably, these K3 surfaces can be distinguished using their distinct elliptic fibrations, especially those originating from different periods of their automorphisms' action on moduli. In particular, this research uncovers instances of K3 surfaces with automorphisms exhibiting Siegel disks of various multiplicities (greater than, equal to, and less than $2$. Moreover, this study challenges the long-standing conjecture posited by Makowski-Miller that K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks must also possess hyperbolic moduli. To achieve this, the authors examine hypergeometric groups associated with these K3 surfaces, compute their growth rates, and investigate the transcendence of calculated algebraic numbers via Leverrier methods, ultimately showing that all K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks are inherently transcendental. The underlying approach employs Lefschetz-type formulas to determine Lefschetz numbers and their corresponding residues. As a result, this research not only resolves Makowski-Miller conjecture but also allows for the computation of Siegel disk multiplicities in previously developed examples. In contrast, this study confirms the validity of a distinct conjecture proposed by Makowski-Miller at the Picard number of $16$. The distinguishing characteristic of K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks lies in their inherent transcendence. Building upon this, the authors explore and analyze explicit examples of K3 surfaces with automorphisms possessing pseudo-Siegel disks, characterized by a Lefschetz number of $(-1/2, 1/2)$, derived from their action on fixed points. These examples challenge a distinct conjecture proposed by Makowski-Miller, specifically with regards to the Lefschetz number's parity. Ultimately, this research not only resolves Makowski-Miller conjecture but also yields significant advancements in the explicit examples of K3 surfaces with both Siegel disks and pseudo-Siegel disks. The main contribution of this research involves developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme for finding the minimum surface topography (genus and non-orientable genus) for complex network graphs that are dense. Currently, a reliable approximation method for determining surface topography in dense graphs only guarantees an error of 1, whereas methods for other graph types offer closer to optimal results. By incorporating a novel random surface sampling approach, we have devised an EPAS algorithm that accurately identifies the surface topography for dense graphs within a constant distance from optimal results, focusing on the minimum surface topography in half-planes and disc surfaces, and extending to other surface models like cylinders and tori, achieving an approximation factor close to 2. This achievement provides an optimal approximation guarantee for dense graphs in various surface models. Our test cases using artificial and real-world networks demonstrate the effectiveness of the EPAS algorithm in determining the surface topography for dense graphs. Furthermore, a related lower bound theorem for surface topography approximation has been established, stating that an approximation factor lower than 1.5 is not feasible for certain graph types. Importantly, our study reveals that dense graphs, particularly those resembling a torus, exhibit surface topography characteristics distinct from those of other graph types. Our analysis provides insights into the properties of dense graphs, enabling us to develop an efficient approximation method for surface topography determination. A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by extensive numerical experiments. Logistic regression scalability benefits from this approach over more widely used distributed algorithms like SGD and DA-DUO at equivalent communication frequencies. Experimental results show stochastic Newton converging faster in many cases than projected gradient methods previously considered optimally convergent. Numerical validation further reveals the new algorithm outperforms existing distributed methods while efficiently utilizing communication resources. Empirical results for both distributed and single-machine scenarios are presented. A related Java-based VASMS framework supports implementing the proposed algorithm. Detailed, step-by-step resource setup guides is provided. In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of moving nuclei resulting from nucleon transfer reactions is crucial. This capability enables researchers to calculate properties such as the reduction factor for nucleon charge, the value of the nucleon spin, and the mass of the $\Lambda$ baryon when in combination with its spin. Although some low-recoil HDTPC detectors have successfully measured these properties, existing high-recoil ones cannot due to limitations in their design. This study proposes certain improvements to HDTPC detectors that would allow them to identify the direction of moving nuclei even at high recoil energies. Researchers simulated and analyzed different scenarios using both simple and directional point scatterers, finding that specific conditions could result in nearly 100% of these events being identifiable. This experiment used single photons to calculate the positions of both the initial and final nuclei, with the angle of motion calculated from these positions. Additionally, researchers found that identifying the direction of moving ions is equivalent to identifying the angle between the paths of both ions. This method was further validated by simulating more realistic conditions based on experiments involving transfer reactions, ultimately resulting in nearly 100% of these events being identifiable. This research serves as a foundation for future experiments focused on nucleon recoil identification, with potential applications including the use of higher voltages and more complex designs on HDTPC detectors to further improve their capabilities. With these improvements, HDTPC detectors have the potential to be used in a wider array of applications. Researchers are currently planning an experiment involving the simulation of non-relativistic transfer reactions using both simulated and real data, with real data obtained from an HDTPC used in the simulation of $\p$ on $^{4}$He reactions at 235 MeV, where angles of both ions were identified in 88$\%$ of $\p$ stopping events. This upcoming experiment is set to be used to calculate properties for both protons and $\Lambda$ baryons. This research, with its proposed improvements and potential applications, serves as an important step towards more accurate calculations of mass for the $\Lambda$ baryon. This specific calculation of mass for the $\Lambda$ baryon, with its proposed method and potential experiments, serves as an important area of study. However, mass for the $\Lambda$ baryon, with its proposed value of 1115.3 MeV, had already been calculated in experiments involving muon-electron conversion, where it was determined that this conversion results in no net change to the mass of the electron.

This paper reports on the findings from the Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge held in conjunction with the 2021 Workshop on Adversarial Robustness. The goal of the challenge was to evaluate how well well-known, widely used neural network classifiers were able to predict less common categories when training data contained fewer examples of these less common categories. Specifically, the challenge posed a problem to model developers to improve their ability to accurately predict less common categories in real-world applications, given that many such classifications fall outside of commonly seen categories in the training data. Detailed results from the challenge, inclduing control group findings, are presented. A companion paper titled "Out-of-Vocabulary Challenge: How Much Training Data is Enough?" provides a more in-depth analysis. Key findings from the challenge include: 1) There was little to no difference in accuracy between the training and predictions for the most common categories, 2) Considerably fewer examples of less common categories are needed to achieve similar accuracy as for more common categories, 3) A substantial data science influenced bias exists and 4) Small variances in hyperparameters result in significant variances in performance across different models. The results from the challenge have significant implications for the way data is pre-processed and how accuracy metrics are chosen for more common vs less common categories in real-world applications. Random fields in mathematical models depict various situations and systems across multiple scales, encompassing applications from physics, engineering, and biology. A random field is considered a geometric random field if its level-set surfaces form a smooth manifold. This paper explores the properties of random field manifolds and their shortest paths. We introduce a local coordinate system using tangent and normal vectors, derived from local minima and maxima. In this framework, we compute the shortest paths, which exhibit geometrically significant characteristics, and demonstrate their potential as novel image segmentation techniques. Moreover, our results can be used to establish some stochastic geometry principles, similar to those found in physics. We also provide new insights into the distribution of extrema along these shortest paths. This research was facilitated by a novel and efficient computational method for calculating the shortest paths, which has broader applications. The adaptive spectral Koopman method was developed to solve complex autonomous dynamical systems that serve as the groundwork for numerous applications across diverse scientific and engineering fields. Despite its high accuracy, ASK has a computational disadvantage in dealing with multi-dimensional systems compared to traditional integration methods like Runge-Kutta. To address this limitation, we introduced a new approach that combines the ASK method with sparse grid techniques to accelerate computation for high-dimensional systems. This innovation, sparse-grid ASK, leverages the strengths of both methods to achieve improved performance and make complex systems more feasible for computation. Our numerical experiments successfully demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of sASK in solving multi-dimensional scientific and engineering problems. Furthermore, we use a challenging multi-scale autonomous system to compare the computational resources required for precise results, and we find that the sparse grid approach significantly reduces the computational burden, making the solution time proportional to the number of degrees of freedom. Additionally, we apply the sASK method to a real-world problem, such as the simulation of quasi-periodic vibration in a parametrically forced Lennard-Jones system, and obtain highly accurate and computationally efficient results. Overall, the sparse-grid ASK method offers a powerful solution for the analysis and prediction of complex high-dimensional systems in various application domains. The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem. While it's well-documented that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, a linear convergence rate is achieved only if both the solution and the solution's gradient are unique. This paper demonstrates that an asymptotic point achieved by the Sinkhorn algorithm can still be a stationary point with a potentially multiplicative influence. This discovery enables the derivation of theoretical convergence proofs for specific problem configurations, including cases where values or marginals are nondistinct and potentially zero. This reasoning is further applied to a scenario where m = 2, a situation where a distinct solution is known to be impossible. This example highlights the importance of monitoring algorithm-produced stationary points for uniqueness when designing convergence arguments. This paper also introduces and demonstrates a generalized version of the Sinkhorn algorithm, referred to as the Adapt-Sinkhorn algorithm, which includes procedures to achieve unique stationary points, achieve linear convergence, and ensure stability against perturbations in data. This algorithm is demonstrated to be effective in various settings including cases with or without solution uniqueness. Numerical experiments are performed to demonstrate the Adapt-Sinkhorn algorithm's performance in a scenario where the solution is known to be unique. This example highlights the Adapt-Sinkhorn algorithm's potential as a robust and reliable solution to the Schrödinger problem, even in scenarios where a solution's existence is uncertain. This paper also demonstrates the Adapt-Sinkhorn algorithm's applicability to additional problem settings, including a scenario where the solution's regularity is constrained. This example highlights the Adapt-Sinkhorn algorithm's potential as a versatile and reliable solution to a wide variety of regularized optimal transport problems. The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various sizes of geometric patterns - ranging from organic life forms to DNA and proteins - across different scales. Chiral matter responds to chiral light with specific polarization properties that allow for the identification and separation of enantiomers within molecular pairs. Developing an optical cavity that preserves and efficiently utilizes chirality, on the other hand, is crucial for operations like chiral sensing and data storage. We present a novel optical cavity design, called the single-handedness chiral cavity, that maintains and takes advantage of the inherent geometry of chiral structures, specifically when based on Snowflake lattices, to support chiral eigenmodes at chiral near-field wavelengths. This innovative design of cavity has the potential to facilitate chiral sensing and the efficient storage of chiral information. We have successfully applied the concept to achieve chiral contrast in Raman sensing between left- and right-handed handedness of a cavity, as confirmed experimentally. A comprehensive numerical model has also been developed to investigate properties of chiral cavities and their dependence on chirality and geometry. As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, predicting and resolving issues, and fulfilling their goal of becoming smart cities due to limited understanding of their infrastructure's current state. Most cities lack accurate digital data on their underground systems (electricity, water, natural gas), hindering construction project planning. To overcome these obstacles, a new framework called GUIDES has been introduced to manage and process data for underground infrastructure systems. This enables a wide range of users - administrators, workers, and the general public - to make data-driven decisions by accessing integrated and digitized information. This transport pipeline connects various data sources (maps, spreadsheets), processes the data (geolocation, validation, and visualization), and displays the combined data on an interactive map. Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. For decades, researchers have disputed the underlying cause of the significant entropy change, whether it stems from the system's vibrational, rotational, and translational entropy or the balance between them. Using neutron spectroscopy and extensive first-principles simulations combined with an entropy analysis approach, we find that the significant entropy originates from the system's rotational and translational entropy of the ammonium ions. This finding highlights the importance of a comprehensive entropy analysis approach. Although the system's 180 K ferroelectric transition is thermodynamically induced, it's primarily driven by the system's rotational and translational entropy, leading to a ferrielectric order being unfavorable below this critical point. During reinforcement learning, humans often adjust their actions in response to unexpected outcomes, using past experiences to forecast future results. While expert learners strive for optimal decisions, less experienced learners might adopt suboptimal strategies. In this study, we examined various learning approaches, including a trait-like strategy, in a group of novices and explored how these behaviors compare to their brain activity while learning. We discovered that both suboptimal and trait-like learners tend to make similar choices when unexpected, and these patterns are reflected in their brain function. In contrast, experienced learners' brain activity, but not behavior, matches that of novice trait-learners. These findings indicate that both suboptimal and trait-like learning styles exist across individuals and suggest potential similarities between these patterns and a brain mechanism. We propose that these distinct approaches to learning may involve different brain processes and that further research on these patterns could reveal more about the underlying cognitive mechanisms. In the future, it may be beneficial to explore the effectiveness of targeted learning interventions, aimed at modifying these strategies, and assessing their impact on the underlying brain processes. To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the trade-off between scalability and reliability; methods that effectively reduce noise on current devices tend to become increasingly inaccurate as more qubits are added. In this research, an advanced MEM method is proposed that combines reverse-design and counteractive strategies. Through a novel iterative unfolding approach, this method can eliminate measurement distortions while retaining high reliability at an expanded scale. Our study indicates that the proposed method not only maintains accuracy in larger systems but can also achieve more precise results in operations requiring many output outcomes, such as the Simon problem. Furthermore, this method outperforms existing MEM methods, including those based on neural networks, in a broad range of scenarios. One of the key advantages of this method is its ability to operate effectively without modifying the measurement process, making it compatible with a wide variety of quantum hardware. In line with these findings, this research recommends implementing the proposed method to enhance the reliability of noisy quantum computers with up to fifty qubits.  Preliminary experiments using noisy Simon algorithm have shown that the proposed method yields an average 2.7-fold enhancement in output accuracy over current error correction methods.  Furthermore, this method exhibits a 4.2-fold and 5.6-fold improvement in output accuracy compared to the best existing error correction methods on twenty-qubit and fifty-qubit systems, respectively.  In addition to its practical applications, this method has significant theoretical implications, such as enhancing the computational power of quantum algorithms and expanding the usable range of quantum hardware.  One of its key theoretical benefits is the ability to efficiently eliminate measurement distortions even on extremely large systems. As robots increasingly share tasks with humans, it has become crucial for them to establish conventions that are understandable to people. In situations where humans and robots collaborate together, these conventions should be clearly communicated. Currently, learning robotic conventions mainly relies on observing human behavior, but this poses difficulties when humans and robots work together, as they tend to cooperate more closely in such shared tasks. Our solution involves employing attention to detail and creates predictable patterns in human-robot collaboration. We demonstrate this approach with a study involving a collaborative driving task, where participants direct the robot to reach a destination while it follows a convention for keeping to its side of the road. By analyzing user input, it becomes apparent that humans respond better to explicit instructions given by the robot as early as possible and that considering prior experiences can lead to more effective collaboration, resulting in reduced latency in robot responses. However, it's also evident that humans expect greater consistency from robots in such shared tasks, as over-reliance on prior experiences leads to significant delays in robot responses, which may undermine collaboration. Our research contributes to the understanding of how communication and prior experiences impact collaborative tasks and paves the way for further exploration of the implications of established robotic conventions on human-robot interaction. It sheds light on the effects of prior experiences and robot behavior on expectations and behavior in shared tasks, while highlighting the role of language as a crucial factor in achieving efficient collaboration between humans and robots. Ultimately, it's essential for robots to be responsive and provide clear explanations, taking into account prior experiences and their own behavior to effectively participate in shared tasks. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the presence of nonlocality and spillover actually minimize these issues, so they have a beneficial effect in this specific context. We further explore how these models can be applied to a wider range of systems beyond quantum hydrodynamics' validity. We analyze the implications of a quantum hydrodynamics model with a finite hydrodynamic wave length on plasmon behavior and reveal that a quantum hydrodynamics model with a reasonable wave length of several nanometers accurately replicates the outcomes of a quantum response theory, thereby providing a valuable approximation. This work's findings have significant potential to deepen our understanding of the behavior of light and electrons at the nanoscale. Importantly, these insights could be applied in designing nanostructures, such as those supporting the Tamm and Hirschfeld surfaces, in order to yield nondiverging and highly confined gap plasmons, thereby enhancing their applications in optics and electronics. For instance, in optics, these plasmons could support highly confined and intense light waves that can be utilized for molecular spectroscopy and imaging, whereas in electronics, they could be used to develop highly sensitive and localized superconducting qubits. Moreover, these findings could be applied in the development of highly efficient and stable photovoltaic devices, such as those integrating a metal and a p-n junction semiconductor, by reducing energy loss and increasing the localization of gap plasmons. Photogeneration of charge and excitations in such a system can be efficiently coupled to the electromagnetic field by increasing the localization of gap plasmons, thereby enhancing the photovoltacic efficiency. In order to develop these ideas, we further investigate the case of a van der Waals crystal-silver structure in which the electron spillover and nonlocal behavior strongly influence its optical properties, particularly as the crystal is very thin. This investigation could be relevant in the development of new photovoltaic devices, such as those integrating a metal and a p-n junction semiconductor, by reducing energy loss and increasing the localization of gap plasmons. Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When dealing with multi-variable data sets, particularly those in longitudinal studies and health contexts, traditional statistical tools often provide complete information, yet make it difficult to incorporate new data without losing focus on existing trends. To address this, we aim to develop an interactive system capable of seamlessly integrating new time-based data into an existing picture. Our solution lies in the intelligent use of data diminishment, an approach influenced by concepts from information visualization, coupled with the integration of user-defined variables via composite parabolic functions. This method allows for an effortless exploration of new data by adjusting dimensionality, while maintaining a clear understanding of how new observations affect existing trends. To showcase our approach, we have created HTSlyzer, an open-source platform enabling effective analysis of combined longitudinal data sets. HTSlyzer's effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of practical examples highlighting its practical applications. Furthermore, we have conducted a comprehensive user study, involving 32 participants, to assess the interactivity aspects involved in analyzing multi-variable data sets. Based on our research findings, we have developed a series of guidelines, aimed at guiding developers and researchers, to facilitate the effective visualization and exploration of time-based data. Our study's discoveries provide a wealth of knowledge, offering diverse avenues for further exploration and research. Ultimately, we have established HTSlyzer as an innovative, interactive tool, offering a groundbreaking solution, previously unattained in comparable systems. The present paper marks the first comprehensive account of HTSlyzer, a statistical data analysis tool. The increasing use of electronic health records (EHRs) poses significant privacy concerns. One potential solution is the federated learning framework, which aims to analyze these records without compromising their security. However, prior research has struggled to account for the heterogeneous connections and varying levels of data availability within the EHR dataset. To address this, a new federated learning method is developed, using a graph neural network to analyze EHR data from multiple institutions and incorporating variable data quantities into the calculation of node similarities. Initial results on synthetic data demonstrate the proposed method's ability to outperform other approaches, and it is subsequently applied to a real-world hospital dataset, yielding promising outcomes in predictive analysis. Overall, the research demonstrates a significant advancement in the field of federated learning, and the resulting approach holds potential for analyzing diverse healthcare datasets. This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique. A direct link is established between a broad-spectrum energy efficiency metric and system design variables including relay placement, scheduling, and power allocation, with these variables combined into a single, decodable signal. By optimizing energy efficiency through a simple mathematical approach, we derive a baseline for comparison and show that a more complex, yet more energy-efficient method, has a high probability of achieving nearly optimal results. Numerical analysis demonstrates the method's effectiveness and highlights its potential benefits in complex communication scenarios. Furthermore, we show that our method is computationally efficient, taking much less time to solve than other approaches, such as cross-entropy optimization. A possible extension to this work could explore the application of machine learning techniques to optimize energy efficiency in communication systems. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed for YSR states formed by single and dual magnetic atoms attached to a superconducting surface. Utilizing density functional theory, this new framework accurately models YSR state characteristics, including energy, sublattice magnetization, and spin polarization. As a crucial component of this method, an analytical model of the YSR state was created by integrating relativistic electron behavior principles. Implementing this approach, researchers successfully replicated numerous experimental findings related to Mn atoms or clusters on Nb(110), including various spin polarizations. Moreover, this approach allowed for the prediction of YSR double-peak patterns resulting from in-plane spin orientations. Finally, in-line with recent experimental discoveries, this assessment predicted a significant energy gap in YSR states for in-plane spin orientations as opposed to out-of-plane spin orientations. Overall, this assessment highlights the value of accounting for the YSR state's complex behavior when interpreting experimental findings, including energy spectra, magnetization, and spin-polarized images of magnetic atoms or clusters on superconducting surfaces. By combining this assessment with scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, researchers may uncover previously hidden information about YSR states and enhance their understanding of the underlying physics. For example, recent experimental findings of Mn dimers on Nb(110) are used to make precise predictions regarding YSR state behavior. These predictions include energy and sublattice magnetization patterns that can be verified through future x-ray photoemission spectroscopy experiments. Moreover, this assessment shows that the observed YSR states of Mn dimers exhibit distinct behavior as a result of their complex magnetic properties, and predictively describe their individual and combined magnetic atom interactions with the superconducting surface. As a result, researchers may use this assessment to explore and classify various YSR states of multiple magnetic atoms or clusters on superconducting surfaces, and identify potential applications for novel quantum devices, including those based on the Kondo effect. Importantly, the proposed theory is expected to significantly contribute to ongoing discussions regarding the nature of YSR states of Mn atoms or clusters on Nb(110) and other related superconducting surfaces, and facilitate future experimental designs to validate quantum behavior in these systems. Moreover, the proposed theory is expected to significantly expand current understanding of YSR states of magnetic atoms or clusters and related quantum phenomena, and facilitate future experimental and theoretical investigations of novel quantum systems with similar characteristics. Overall, the proposed theory is expected to significantly enhance theoretical and experimental descriptions of YSR states and related quantum phenomena, and facilitate future research in this field.

This compact data remains readable by the selfsame 3D LiDAR sensor, facilitating quick online processing via a deep neural network (DNN) built with TensorFlow. As localized, handheld scanning is commonly performed offline, an offline optimization technique utilizing a DNN has been developed to minimize compression artifacts. Finally, an empirical analysis of the described methods yields guidelines for the selection of relevant parameters, including a discussion of their potential applications. These proposals include experimenting with an adjustable metric to balance optimization time and image quality. Moreover, employing a DNN filter offers an additional advantage: enabling bias-reduced ODE-based rotation estimation by storing rotating feature maps separately from static ones. This is made possible by storing the DNN activation maps for static features through offline optimization and excluding them in subsequent online processing, thus minimizing temporal correlations in rotation estimates. This finding sheds light on the structural and temporal properties of neural network responses, revealing valuable insights for future optimization work. Cross-disciplinary collaboration between machine learning and dynamical systems researchers has yielded numerous breakthroughs, leading to innovative data-driven approaches for prediction and control. However, traditional dynamical systems methods are still preferred in many scientific and engineering applications. One major drawback of relying solely on dynamical systems methods is the inherent assumption that model error can be characterized by random disturbances. When this assumption does not hold, model-based predictive control may produce suboptimal results. Machine learning, on the other hand, holds promise for identifying error patterns without requiring knowledge of a dynamical model. Despite this potential, there is a lack of coordination between machine learning and control communities, resulting in disparate numerical methods and applications that make it difficult to compare results. To bridge this gap, we develop a framework that integrates machine learning and control, assuming access to a large dataset but no prior knowledge of a dynamical system. Our goal is to identify a function that accounts for model error, enabling the use of learned models for closed-loop control. Our study begins with a theoretical analysis of model error, followed by the presentation of two machine learning methods for identifying error functions under two distinct constraint settings. Finally, we examine our findings in three different applications. Our framework is available on GitHub under the repository name ML-ME. when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.

Given the availability of causal analysis tools, we can utilize these methods to identify dimensions critical to the remaining 10% of the population not receiving HIV care, ultimately informing targeted interventions. Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen escalating interest in community. The appearance of pre-trained visual and language models has significantly accelerated its advancement. However, the existing models based on pre-trained visual and language knowledge often suffer from two major drawbacks. Firstly, the multi-modal features learned through pre-text tasks are not directly aligned with the query of the main task. Secondly, the inefficient fusion of pre-trained visual and language features leads to lost information or ransoming effect. To address the two issues, we present TS2-Net, a text-video retrieval framework that combines a novel token shifting mechanism with a selection transformer. The token shifting mechanism is designed to dynamically realign the token positions in the visual feature map based on text cues, enhancing their matching potential. A selection transformer is then applied to learn feature attention for efficient fusion, by allowing the selection of key visual tokens by text guidance, and allowing the selection of relevant textual words by visual cues. Experiments on various challenging benchmarks, such as ActivityNet and HTC, validate the effectiveness of our approach, and our TS2-Net establishment of new benchmarks with our model, and our model outperforms the previous best approach, MediaFusion. The details of our method, including code and models, are made available to the public. For instance, our model's code is publicly available at this link https://github.com/whwu1025/TS2-Net. Our model won the ActivityNet 2019 competition and the MediaFusion challenge at the ACM Multimedia 2019 conference. In numerous Machine Learning applications, selecting an optimal kernel function is a pivotal step. Gaussian Processes excel in regression and classification tasks, largely depending on a chosen kernel. While there are numerous kernels at disposal, little is known regarding the best kernel for a specific problem. We present GPE, a novel Gaussian Process kernel generator that produces kernels from fundamental mathematical expressions. We implement an Evolutionary Algorithm to create kernels, combining successful algorithms to evolve complex mathematical expressions. The results, obtained on real-world datasets, demonstrate that GPE-produced kernels surpass the standard ones. Moreover, we investigate GPE-produced kernels in Artificial Neural Networks and Regularized Gaussian Process Regression, highlighting their potential as a separate machine learning approach. Further, we introduce GP:INN, a revolutionary architecture that integrates GPE-produced kernels and Inferring Neural Networks. The experimental outcomes reveal that GP:INN consistently surpasses traditional Gaussian Process performance. Consequently, our contributions aim to enhance GPE-produced kernels and related methods, such as GP:INN, as standalone Machine Learning techniques. We strongly believe that GPE-produced kernels warrant further exploration in various Machine Learning domains. The primary code is written in Python, employing the following libraries: GaussianProcess as a Gaussian Process classifier tool, skopt for hyper-parameter optimization, DEAP for the DE algorithm, and PyGNN for deep Gaussian process models. Python's sympy library manages the symbolic expressions used within GPE. We encourage potential users to expand our research into novel areas, including GPE-produced kernel applications. The full Python code for GPE and related methods, including source files, can be found at https://github.com/ivanovap/GPE-INCORE. background interference will hinder accurate data analysis and detector
operation unless mitigated. Research focuses on reducing BIB in detector design,
including triggering, data processing, and analysis stages. Studies were carried
out on a detector utilizing a tungsten nose-cone to filter BIB for a 1.5 TeV
energy threshold. In-depth analysis targeted the innermost detector sections with
highest densities, while conceptual design proposals aimed to optimize a
calorimeter for efficient BIB suppression. Additionally, an advanced trigger
algorithm was developed to identify BIB, leveraging a deep neural network and
expansion of a detector model to include the tungsten nose-cone. Preliminary
results indicated successful BIB identification and reduction, achieving a
significant suppression benefit with further optimization expected. It is
projected that these methods can lower BIB rates to desirable levels for
detector operation. This work will be presented at the 2021 Joint American
Physical Society and Division of Nuclear Physics Meeting in a proposed addition
to the "Beam Induced Backgrounds at Muon Colliders" discussion session. The
