Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity. This method effectively leverages a flexible, differentiable sparsity metric called the Spartan metric. This metric measures the distance between a network and a target configuration with specified sparse features. Spartan is taken from a family of Regulated Transportation (RegTran) metrics. This work demonstrates Spartan on various tasks and networks, showing cross-mapping can be eliminated and significantly more sparsity can be achieved than with Thresholding. Spartan offers several benefits including the ability to train networks from any initial state, visibility into the desired features, and the ability to target specific sub-networks. Additionally, many Spartan optimizations are applicable to other RegTran methods. Spartan's open-source implementation is available on GitHub. This paper explores Spartan in depth on the task of Pruning and SubNet Extraction. It shows that Spartan achieves 70% sparsity on ResNet20, 79% sparsity on ResNet50, and 87% sparsity on VGG16. Additionally, it shows that Spartan can extract 93% of the accurate subnetworks from the massive 224 layer ConvNeXt-B model through a very small additional layer, and shows that these subnetworks are generalizable and robust against adversarial attacks. This paper also and demonstrates many additional benefits of the RegTran family. By training only the last layer, and using the RegTran as a regularizer, it shows an additional 1% improvement in accuracy and 18% sparsity in the well-tuned ConvNeXt-B model. Similarly, it shows an 8% accuracy improvement and 6% sparsity in the less-optimal ResNet50 model. Additionally, it shows that regressing towards a model of the correct class, rather than a completely sparse model, yields a 100% warrant of the desired features and 40% improvement in accuracy and sparsity. Lastly, it shows that using the RegTran as a constraint rather than a penalty yields similar or better results than training without the constraint. This research demonstrates the potential for the RegTran family to tackle a wide variety of tasks and motivations. It shows that various combinations of constraints and objectives are possible, and that many optimizations that work for Spartan and other RegTran methods also work for other distribution distances. The requirement for containing a Bose-Einstein condensate forces many-body theories to be treated numerically from a few thousand atoms onwards in contemporary publications. Consequently, the contribution of single-body and two-body interparticle interactions that become relevant at smaller scales are often overlooked in these studies. In order to incorporate the effects of repulsive atom-atom interactions in theoretical models, this work adopts an unorthodox approach by employing a simple mean-field Hartree method to simulate a weakly correlated Bose gas composed of spin-polarized hydrogen atoms. By comparing the predicted phase diagram of superfluid hydrogen to experimental data collected by Dieckemann et al. in 2008, we demonstrate that incorporating the effects of repulsive atom-atom interactions results in a notable advancement in the development of Bose-Einstein condensation. Furthermore, the predicted density of states in the superfluid phase, obtained through this study, displays a distinct gap-like structure near the Fermi level that is analogous to the Pauli blocking phenomenon, commonly observed in itinerant ferromagnets. However, the emergence of this gap is solely attributed to the effects of repulsive atom-atom interactions, the principle of Pauli blocking, and the characteristics of Bose-Einstein condensation. Importantly, the present study is capable of simulating Bose-Einstein condensation at much lower atom numbers than numerical many-body theories, thereby facilitating an accurate description and understanding of associated phenomena like the Pauli blocking effect. The predicted density of states, also experimentally measurable, provides an accessible means of validating the accuracy of simplified models used to describe superfluid hydrogen through direct comparison with data. In particular, we anticipate that our predicted density of states, obtained through the use of a mean-field Hartree method, will be found to be in agreement with data, while the phenomenon of Pauli blocking is observed to be diminished at higher atom densities. In order to verify these predictions, we intend to access existing data collected using a variety of experimental techniques like NMR, Andreev reflection, radio-frequency spectroscopy, Bragg spectroscopy, among others, used to study hydrogen at ultra-low temperatures. In conclusion, the present study is poised to significantly contribute to the evolution of simplified models used to describe Bose-Einstein condensation, thereby facilitating an accurate understanding and description of associated phenomena like the Pauli blocking effect. Importantly, the study is expected to significantly impact the description and understanding of superfluidity using theoretical models, thereby bridging the gap between numerical many-body theories and experimental studies on hydrogen at low concentrations

However, it has been observed that test code can degrade over time, giving rise to test smells that negatively impact maintainability. Although these problems exist, there is a shortage of scientific research investigating the issues from the perspectives of software developers. A key reason for this deficiency is the lack of a clear definition of test smells and a corresponding methodology for identifying them. A recent study addressed these gaps by providing an empirical framework for identifying test smells in real-world projects. A follow-up study has now analyzed the perspective of software developers on the defined test smells, drawing insights from interviews with participants. Specifically, this study examined developers' interpretations of the defined test smells, their acknowledged presence in tested code, their perceived severity, and proposed solutions to rectify test smells. Interestingly, while software developers were aware of the defined test smells, they did not consider them to be severe issues. Notably, although test smells were recognized as suboptimal, they were not viewed as major obstacles by the developers. A significant finding was that developers were unsure of how to address test smells in tested code. We introduce the updated version of the {\tt KKMCee} event generator, version 5.00.2, designed for simulating lepton and quark pair production through high-energy electron-positron annihilations. As the most advanced generator for this process, the code, now rewritten entirely in modern C++, maintains all features of its Fortran 77 predecessor, while incorporating several enhanced Monte Carlo algorithm improvements. Its capabilities, supplemented with next-to-leading order QED corrections, genuine weak corrections using the {\tt TOPDRAWER2} program, and various photon spectrum descriptions, provide the highest accuracy available today (exceeding 1000 times finer than in the 1990s) and are now combined in a single, user-friendly tool. This is particularly beneficial in the context of future lepton colliders, where the need for precise $W$ and $Z$ boson production predictions may arise. Moreover, the code is now capable of simulating final states involving polarized initial-state electrons, implemented through the {\tt POLPHO} Monte Carlo algorithm. This is particularly significant for the currently discussed Higgs Factory, where precise $\mathrm{e^+e^-\to HZ}$ decays, requiring realistic polarized $\mathrm{e^+e^-}$ initial states, may play a crucial role. Finally, the code is now able to simulate high-energy $\mathrm{e^+\to e^-f\bar{f}}$ decays, allowing for the investigation of rare effects, while the inclusion of {\tt PHOSPHOR} enabled the introduction of a user-friendly $\mathrm{e\to e'\gamma}$ description. This is now combined with several other important features, including beam-polarization effects in a universal and easy-to-use manner. Our investigation into a $^7$H resonant state treated as a five-body system with a $^3$H core and four neutrons involved, was conducted utilizing the hyperspherical approach.  Through a novel method of generating the $^3$H+4n resonance state from a more manageable $^3$H+4n resonance configuration, it became possible to overcome the difficulties associated with constructing the $^7$H ground state, which has duality properties, from two-body effective potentials only.  Our calculated estimates for the $^7$H ground state, including its energy, certain form factors, and other properties, were found to be in relatively good agreement with existing experimental data.  Additionally, quasiparticle wave functions derived from this model were used to calculate various $^7$H decay widths to gamma rays and neutrons.  Effective masses of neutrons and protons within this system were determined by analyzing the kinetic energies of neutrons and protons, and were found to be decreasing in a manner consistent with the distance from the $^3$H core.  Our findings were discussed in the context of a possible H-like ground state for the $^8$H isotope.  To validate our five-body model description of the $^7$h, we compared it to a six-body model involving a $^3$H+4n+1g configuration, and found that incorporating a very minor configuration involving a $^4$He impurity was necessary to reconcile the two models at the level of quasiparticle wave functions.  Our analysis revealed that this $^4$He impurity has a very small energy and is not detectable in either the five-body or six-body systems.  Our study provides a model for the $^7$H ground state that is relatively stable and accurately accounts for existing experimental data.  This model has the potential to be extended to other light hydrogen and light neutron-rich isotopes.  Specifically, we were able to describe the $^8$H isotope using our models and various experimental data. In various fields of scientific inquiry, a common challenge exists in assessing the effects of interventions on multiple units and outcomes using time-series data from observational settings. To address this issue, we've devised a novel method combining established approaches based on the factor analysis model with a Bayesian inference framework. Our proposed method uniquely accounts for transient outcomes influenced by interventions and retains flexibility in modeling both transient and permanent outcomes while maintaining identifiability. To apply this method in a novel field, we've examined the impact of local tracing partnerships on the performance of COVID-19 contact tracing in England, a country with 45-60 intervention groups and an 8-week follow-up period. Our findings suggest that local tracing partnerships have a significant and timely effect on increasing the diary coverage and self-reporting outcomes, and contact isolation, as confirmed by a diagnostic model assessing common causes of association and temporal correlation. To provide a more comprehensive understanding, we've also applied a model integrating all outcomes and explored alternative models for sensitivity analysis. Our results can serve as a starting point for future evaluations of the effect of local tracing partnerships, and the proposed method can be widely applied to analyze time-series data from various interventions and settings. Furthermore, our work offers a methodical approach for contact tracing evaluation, a field that has received limited attention in research. To address this limitation, we've also considered a model extending the factor analysis model with a hierarchical structure, accounting for transient and permanent outcomes, and incorporating additional covariates for enhanced model performance and interpretability. A prospective evaluation of the effect of local tracing partnerships has been missing from the literature, and our work fills this gap with a comprehensive analysis of the effect of these partnerships and a novel method for time-series data analysis. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated whether it's feasible to calculate the necessary camera calibration parameters directly from a single image, eliminating the need for 3D reconstruction and real-time recalibration. Our innovative approach involves deriving intrinsic parameters by analyzing the image and extrinsic parameters by comparing it to a previously calculated pose, making it the first method to calculate eye-in-hand camera calibration from a single image, even in pose-agnostic cases. Our algorithm's performance in simulated and real-world scenarios, as demonstrated by the ROBOSUB competition results, shows that it outperforms established methods and achieves accurate calibration across various conditions. Our source code is freely accessible online.

In real-world settings, RL systems face difficulties due to constraints on their actions, such as due to costly movements or physical limitations. To deploy RL in such environments, it's essential to create optimal reward schemes that these systems can utilize. This requirement prompts the development of a new RL inverse problem, inverse constrained reinforcement learning (ICRL), which aims to identify a reward function that maximizes an agent's expected return when subjected to existing action constraints. To address ICRL, we introduce a new variational inverse problem formulation, demonstrating that under mild conditions, the optimal constrained policy is also the optimal parameterized policy. This insight allows us to develop a scalable algorithm for solving ICRL without policy space limitation. We also establish a connection between ICRL and causal inference and reveal a common framework for several existing RL problems, including causal induction and variational information maximization. Our proposed algorithm is empirically shown to generalize and enhance the performance of ACL, an existing method that addresses the unconstrained RL problem. The growing importance of Adversarial Machine Learning within the ML community cannot be disregarded. In this study, we explore the cross-section of Graph Neural Networks and adversarial attacks, with a particular focus on poisoning attacks on GNNs. We investigate the resilience of GNNs to poisoning attacks during the training process and develop a two-player game model incorporating reinforcement learning. The training sample labels are manipulated by the adversary, and the GNN trainer responds with a GNN model. We represent the GNN training as a Markov decision process, and within this framework, we formulate three GNN fitting tasks as maximization problems within the Adversarial ML framework. We implement and evaluate our approach through experiments on four datasets and compare the outcomes with the existing state-of-the-art method, demonstrating that the proposed model excels at GNN training robustness. We also extend the traditional GNN fit problem to include multiple iterations of the training process, resulting in the development of a dynamic GNN fitting model, where the GNN trainer seeks to build robust models on selected training samples for subsequent training iterations. We experimentally validate the multiple iteration model and showcase its superior performance in providing robustness against poisoning attacks in GNNs. We further introduce a variant of the GNN fitting model in which the GNN trainer seeks to fit the GNN model on multiple selected training samples for successive training iterations, resulting in the creation of a dual fitting model. We experimentally validate the multiple iteration variant and demonstrate its ability to provide robustness against poisoning attacks in GNNs. Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In particular, biomedical ontologies encompass a wide range of relevant concepts, including those related to human diseases, organs, and environmental factors. A significant majority of concepts within these ontologies are connected to only a few other concepts, making it efficient to compute their full association graph. However, visualising and navigating these complex, high-dimensional relationships is challenging due to their three- to five-dimensional structure and large size. To address this issue, we introduce OntoPlot, a novel interactive visualization system that effectively presents the complex associations within large, multi-dimensional concept graphs. OntoPlot first identifies clusters of closely related concepts and then presents each cluster as a circular layout, preserving the hierarchy of hierarchically connected concepts when displaying their associations. By reducing the dimensionality of non-hierarchical concept relationships and removing unnecessary cluster connections, OntoPlot efficiently enables users to visualise and navigate the complex, multi-dimensional associations within large ontologies, making it easier to identify key concepts and their significant associations. The system's efficiency is further enhanced by novel optimisation techniques that quickly identify relevant cluster connections. OntoPlot's performance remains unaffected by the substantial growth of ontology size, allowing users to interact with large ontologies containing tens of thousands of concepts. To showcase its capabilities, we apply OntoPlot to the Human Disease Ontology and the Integrated Taxon ontology. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically leverages inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to bridge the gap between speech and text representations for improved end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss utilizes a discriminator that maps speech to text or vice versa, and we find that training this discriminator with both adversarial and cyclic constraints facilitates more effective feature mapping. Experimental evaluations on the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech datasets demonstrate that our approach, incorporating both inter-domain loss and cyclic constraint, achieves a char-level word error rate reduction of 8% over standard end-to-end automatic speech recognition systems. Furthermore, we observe that the combination of inter-domain loss and cyclic constraint outperforms other methods, including both inter-domain loss-only solutions and cyclic constraint-only systems trained with inter-domain loss. Additionally, we investigate the role of inter-domain loss in the training process and reveal that its impact is greatest during the first optimization stage. Besides, using inter-domain loss alone is most effective when trained over a long period, and we find that system optimized with inter-domain loss and cyclic constraint always outperform inter-domain loss-only systems in all optimization iterations. Thus, our proposed method presents a new, efficient, and powerful solution for improving the accuracy of end-to-end automatic speech recognition systems, especially in environments with limited labeled data. The experiments and analysis provide valuable insights into the behavior of end-to-end automatic speech recognition systems and the characteristics of inter-domain loss and cyclic constraint. Finally, our results highlight the superiority of combining standard training methods with loss and constraint techniques tailored to specific tasks. The proposed method has potential applications in a wide variety of machine learning domains, and we anticipate that our research will inspire more efficient approaches to end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Active Learning strategies, which reduce the volume of data to be labeled, are typically used in scenarios where the cost of annotation is exceedingly high. This research focuses on applying Active Learning strategies to robotics, where autonomous navigation using a map and an ecological model is employed. We introduce a new approach, called DAI, which leverages observations to refine the parameters of an Bayesian Agent, causing it to modify the mapping and route planning strategies. The observed data is obtained via sensors, while the route planning is based on the prediction of future information gain. The goal of DAI is to ensure that both the robot's path and map predictions enable maximum information acquisition regarding the environment. DAI is unique because it integrates perception, prediction, and decision-making into a unified Bayesian framework. When put to the test in a simulated environment, DAI's performance exceeded that of traditional Active Learning methods, while demonstrating remarkable robustness to sensor and annotation inaccuracies. To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into neural machine translation systems, a novel NMT architecture is introduced, which enables the alignment of words and syntactic tree structures during translation. This new architecture, called NMT-TSC, utilizes an additional tree search module to determine optimal word alignments. To ensure that the source and target language syntactic parse trees remain aligned throughout the search process, the system only considers tree structures with two branches, mirroring the left-to-right word-by-word prediction process of conventional NMT systems. This results in a reduced search space, making tree structure decoding feasible. To further streamline the search process, a top-down tree traversal approach is employed, along with a pre-pruning technique to eliminate unnecessary tree structures. This new architecture also outperforms other baseline models in various metrics on the CoNLL 2017 parsing dataset, even serving as a robust dependency parsing method that is particularly insensitive to noisy syntactic annotation. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, especially in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the problem of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. We develop a new meta-algorithm, (TAR)MAC, which learns a "meta-matrix" factorization across related tasks and establishes its first theoretical proof of concealing malicious noise, recovering an accurate underlying linear structure in an adversarial setting. Specifically, for a given number of adversarial tasks, (TAR)MAC demonstrates the ability to recover the low-dimensional linear structure for an number of tasks linear in the number of tasks, while maintaining a constant failure rate. We further extend this result to a more dynamic setting, where each task has a varying level of noise, while maintaining a constant number of tasks. In this setting, (TAR)MAC demonstrates the ability to adapt its parameter space across related tasks, while maintaining linear convergence to achieve a minimally small convex cone angle with the optimal linear structure, while remaining resilient to malicious noise. We further establish that our algorithm's noise resilience stems from a form of statistical query learning, allowing it to extract a interpretable, sparse structure even in the presence of noise. We test the performance of (TAR)MAC on both artificial datasets as well as fMRI-based single-trial prediction studies, observing its noise resilience in the real-world application. As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish clear guidelines for addressing potential harm. A key consideration is the distinction between physical and psychological harm, which poses difficulties due to the interconnectedness of mental and emotional states. A new framework based on causal concepts seeks to address these complexities, emphasizing the concept of causal agency - the ability of a system's actions to cause harm. This new theory defines key terms, including using a novel understanding of the "loss of the chance" concept and incorporating ideas from existing research on actual causality and psychological harm. The approach focuses on physical psychological states, eliminating unnecessary complexities and abstracting from irrelevant mental conditions. The theory's application to various scenarios, including a self-driving car's collision and a physical attack, demonstrates its ability to capture subtleties like pre-existing conditions and psychological fragility. The theory's logical structure enables the derivation of specific formulas and it is shown that this theory aligns with existing moral theories while offering a more coherent account of complex issues. The analysis highlights several practical dilemmas, including potential psychological harm and a system's tendency to cause psychopathic behavior. The theory's application to these scenarios reveals new insights and understandings of the role of causality in explaining harm. The resulting theory offers practical guidance to mitigating harm and highlights important distinctions, such as the difference between a system's ability to cause harm and its actual responsibility for it. The theory's findings suggest that, in some cases, a system's ability to cause harm does not imply its liability for it, and that it is only liable if it was the system's actions that made the difference between the harm's occurrence and non-occurrence. The theory emphasizes the critical role of choosing the correct comparator to ensure just moral accountability in advanced autonomous systems. The analysis concludes by exploring further extensions to the theory, including integrating concepts like intentionality, exploring theories based on the deprivation of value, examining distributive justice and the principle of pro rata distributive justice and more. The resulting ideas and extensions can guide future research in the ethics of autonomous systems and contribute to a more comprehensive and in-depth understanding of the role of causality in explaining harm. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. While individual speech and text pairs can be learned and decoded efficiently, combining speech and text from two distinct languages poses significant difficulties, necessitating extensive labeled data or costly manual annotation. This study proposes a novel approach to speech-to-text translation without requiring annotated data, drawing on the extensive resources available for paired speech and text languages. We leverage a text-to-text model to generate initial translations, which we then fine-tune with unsupervised speech-to-text regularization on a single language. Empirical evidence suggests this strategy yields comparable results to supervised approaches, even with speech and text from two languages that aren't perfectly matched. We also introduce an innovative alignment technique for speech and text from different languages, and provide in-depth analysis of our approach. Experiments on two challenging speech-to-text datasets from various languages demonstrate the effectiveness of our solution. The associated codes are available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ling-gh/zsst. Our experiment design involves: (i) employing a robust ensemble of non-specialized models for translating speech into text, (ii) employing a robust ensemble of non-specialized models for translating text into text in different languages, (iii) using a data-driven approach to translate speech into text across languages through a robust ensemble of non-specialized models. We conduct controlled comparisons of these approaches against each other and against a supervised speech-to-text model. Our experiment demonstrates that the approach that first translates speech into text and then translates text into text across languages yields results comparable to a supervised speech-to-text model. Importantly, our approach enables translation of speech into text across languages without requiring speech-data from the target speech language. Our study provides novel and rigorous insights into the design of zero-shot speech-to-text models. Our work has potential implications for future research on zero-shot speech-to-text models, and may lead to breakthroughs in other multi-lingual tasks such as zero-shot machine translation. The associated codes are available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/linggh/zero-shot-translation. Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated load distributions among a small number of customers, which can vary significantly over the course of a day. Since precise forecasting is challenging due to limited data availability at this scale, an alternative approach involves developing accurate predictions through the combination of multiple forecasts, a technique known as forecast fusion. This study investigates the application of forecast fusion to improve forecasting accuracy for the low voltage market, with a particular focus on enhancing the prediction of daily peak loads, as this value is crucial in network management. We evaluate various forecast fusion techniques, including arithmetic mean and median forecasting methods, as well as an implementation of the Distributed Equal Area Totalization (DATE) method, an established approach to forecast fusion. The analysis suggests that the arithmetic mean forecast averaging method yields superior results on the low voltage scale, as it produces forecasts comparable in quality to those produced by a benchmark model, a Bayesian Neural Network (BNN). Further analysis indicates that incorporating daily peak forecasts into an overall probabilistic prediction system significantly enhances its level of accuracy, as demonstrated by a measurement of the Mean Absolute Error (MAE). We analyze the sensitivity of our forecasts to different levels of data availability, as well as the impact of the choice of time intervals used for the forecasts, a factor of potential significance to the development of future forecasting methods. The analysis suggests that higher levels of data availability lead to improved forecasting accuracy, as may be expected, as well as indicates a range of optimal forecasting intervals, a choice of which may influence the performance of these forecasts. The study's primary contribution lies in the application of forecast fusion techniques to the precise calculation of energy consumption at the low voltage market scale, as well as the study's findings on the impact of data availability and forecasting intervals on the quality of these forecasts. In particular, the issue of occlusion in light field data further complicates the process. Our novel occlusion-aware cost constructor uses a novel design of occlusion-sensitive terms and a carewell-structured cost matrix to address this challenge. We test its performance in the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) LF dataset and the LF-Express dataset. Our constructor outperforms state-of-the-art methods in the field. Our source code is available for reference on the GitHub platform. 

Keywords: light field, depth estimation, matching cost constructor, occlusion, deep learning. 

It's worth noting that traditional machine learning methods have been largely overlooked in light field processing, with the field of deep learning dominating the field. Our novel cost constructor is based on a deep learning approach, specifically the well-known PWC-Net model. Our constructor adds two novel oculation-sensitive terms to the PWC-Net model and develops a carewell-structured cost matrix to address the occlusion issue in light field data.

  - The mean absolute error (MAE) of our constructor and state-of-the-art methods were compared on the Kit LF dataset and the LF-Express dataset.

This study uses the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, first reducing the system and then employing double Wronskian solutions to yield a range of solutions for the reduced equations, resulting in a comprehensive overview of solutions for both classical and nonlocal Fokas-Lenells equations. Several solutions are illustrated through asymptotic analysis, notably, novel solutions are obtained for Fokas-Lenells equations linked to real discrete eigenvalues, previously unreported in analytical methods, and notably one, two, three, four singularities etc. configurations. Furthermore, using conformal mapping, solutions for the continuous Fokas-Lenells equations are obtained, and notably, a new solution is obtained for Lenells equation. A selection of the most prominent solutions are presented. Interestingly, a direct link is observed between Fokas-Lenells equations and the Fokas-Ablowitz-Kadomtsev-Petviashili system, enabling the derivation of solutions for the latter system as well as previously unreported solutions for the Fokas-Ablowitz-Kadomtsev-Petviashili equation. Solutions are further extended to multi-Fokas-Lenells equations and the newly formed multi-Fokas-Ablowitz-Kadomtsev-Petviashili equation. As an added value, a range of periodic solutions for the Fokas-Lenells equations are obtained through conformal mapping from solutions of the 1D Sasa-Satchell equation. Verification of our findings is achieved through direct numerical simulation studies. A notable feature of our work is the derivation of analytic expression for the Fokas-Lenells equation for a selection of configurations using asymptotic analysis, a first in the literature. In the process of our investigation, multiple new bilinear identities for the Fokas-Lenells equations and the continuous 1D Sasa-Satchell equation are derived, and notably a new ordinary differential equation is obtained for Lenells equation. Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explore quantum gravity and model systems with non-relativistic symmetry. However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This technical note utilizes the formulation of double field theory to create action frameworks for these alternative gravity theories. By doing so, it resolves the ambiguities associated with their corresponding motion equations. As a result, this note embeds three theories – Torsional Newton-Cartan gravity, Carrollian gravity, and String Newton-Cartan gravity – within double field theory and derives their respective action frameworks for comparison with previously established literature results. The embedding also simplifies the complexity involved in manually crafting these alternative gravity theories. This approach confirms that action frameworks for Carrollian and String Newton-Cartan gravity were initially defined correctly. However, it corrects an earlier erroneous depiction of the action framework for Torsional Newton-Cartan gravity, suggesting an alternative formulation. The authors note that embedding these alternative gravity theories in double field theory simplifies the process of transitioning them to quantum gravity theories. Moreover, this approach aligns with the formulation of action frameworks for systems featuring non-Riemannian symmetry, including Hořava-Lifshitz, Loop Quantum Gravity, and Causal Dynamical Triangulation theories. The authors speculate that embedding these theories in double field theory may serve as a starting point for a potential transition to quantum gravity, similar to a similar approach for the aforementioned quantum gravity theories. The authors hope this development will inspire novel methodologies in quantum gravity theory transitions in the future. The details and calculations underpinning this note's conclusions are provided. To meet growing demands for next-generation home WiFi networks, it is essential to improve their performance. One effective strategy, known as network selection, involves choosing the best access point (AP) or extender for each device based on available options. By strategically assigning devices to APs or extenders, network performance can be enhanced. In this study, a channel load awareness approach is proposed for AP and extender selection, taking into account their capabilities and operating standards (IEEE 802.11k/v). This proposal utilizes the following metrics to optimize device assignment: the number of APs or extenders reported by devices, the access point's reported number of active devices, the signal strength, and the channel load of each access point. By considering these metrics, the assignment process can be controlled and optimized. The performance of the proposed solution is evaluated using simulations based on real-world scenarios, as well as an actual home WiFi network measurement study, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving network performance and reducing interference. By assigning devices to APs or extenders with sufficient coverage and capacity, the proposed solution helps to prevent performance degradation and improve overall network performance. Additionally, the proposal controls channel access and prevents over-crowding, ensuring fair and stable network access. The study also identifies potential limitations and gray areas of IEEE 802.11k/v standards that contributed to this research. The performance of the proposed solution is evaluated through two main metrics: the number of devices using lower-speed networks and the overall network throughput. By comparing the proposed solution to random assignment, the results show that the proposed solution can reduce 57.1% to 75.1% of lower-speed networks and achieve 42.3% to 71.4% higher throughput. The analysis of the results shows that the proposed solution can effectively improve network performance and reduce interference. The proposed method integrates multiple metrics to optimize network performance and control assignment. By considering channel load and other metrics, the proposed solution can improve device assignment and prevent performance degradation.
